high_priority_articles.title: Fed Minutes Show Another Rate Hike Is Likely This Year as Kevin Warsh's FOMC Battles Persistent Inflation. Here's Why That Signal Matters for Stocks and Bonds Heading Into Year-End. - The Motley Fool
high_priority_articles.summary: Fed Minutes Show Another Rate Hike Is Likely This Year as Kevin Warsh's FOMC Battles Persistent Inflation. Here's Why That Signal Matters for Stocks and Bonds Heading Into Year-End.  The Motley Fool
high_priority_articles.full_text:
According to the latest meeting minutes released Oct. 7 by the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), Kevin Warsh and the other central bankers are planning to hike interest rates again in 2026. The FOMC has two more meetings left this year, Oct. 28 and Dec. 9, to decide on possible Fed rate hikes by year-end.
Inflation seems to be sticking around like an unwanted houseguest. The most recent CPI report showed that consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in September 2026. After raising interest rates in September, it looks like the Fed is going to have to hike by another quarter percentage point or possibly half percentage point by the end of this year.
Let's look at a few high-level impacts of Fed interest rate hikes and what they mean for investors in stocks and bonds.
Higher interest rates: Bad for stocks (usually)
When the Fed hikes interest rates, it's trying to reduce the money supply and slow down the economy. It's trying to make money more expensive, make borrowing more expensive, and hopefully reduce inflation. When there are too many dollars chasing too few goods and services, that drives inflation higher. When there are fewer dollars in the economy, that tends to drive down inflation.
But cutting inflation, while necessary, can be bad in the short run for stock prices. Higher interest rates mean higher borrowing costs. Loans and consumer credit get more expensive. Lots of people might decide not to buy a new car this year, not to apply for a home mortgage, not to open a new credit card. Business leaders make decisions based on higher interest rates, too. Higher costs of business borrowing might make companies decide not to build a new factory, not to hire new employees, not to invest in future growth.
All of this can be bad for stocks. In 2022, the last time the Fed was hiking interest rates aggressively, the S&P 500 index (^GSPC +0.28%) declined by about 19%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 was down about 33%.
We might not be on the verge of that same kind of 2022-style rate-driven stock market crash. Kevin Warsh and the Fed seem to be making smaller adjustments. Stock market investors should be cautious, but not panicking right now. If you're a long-term investor, buying a low-cost index fund like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.31%) could still be a great choice.
Recent research from Vanguard suggests that Fed rate hikes won't hurt the stock market in the short run -- rates might need to go at least a percentage point higher before the stock market would suffer negative effects. There's never a 100% "safe" time to buy stocks, but a few Fed rate hikes right now don't seem like a big enough reason to be bearish.
Higher interest rates: Better for bonds? (maybe)
Warsh and the Fed's FOMC don't control all interest rates -- only the short-term effective federal funds rate. But when the Fed hikes interest rates, longer-term bond yields tend to go higher, too. And when bond yields go up, bond prices go down. Higher rates and lower bond prices can be a sign for investors to "buy the dip" on bonds.
Buying bonds at today's higher rates and lower prices can become a better deal for bond investors. When risk-free U.S. government bond yields are at 5% or higher, that might make many investors stop and think, "Maybe I'd like to buy bonds instead of stocks, and lock in that safe yield."
If you want to buy bonds at today's higher interest rates, the Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF (BND +0.21%) is a simple, low-cost way to put thousands of high-quality U.S. bonds in your portfolio.

European leaders are rethinking their approach to the Kremlin, Financial Times foreign affairs columnist Gideon Rachman writes. More politicians in the European Union now agree that negotiations with Vladimir Putin should not remain the exclusive prerogative of the United States. European countries could soon open their own talks with the Kremlin. Channels of communication are already in place, he says.
EU policy toward Russia has rested on two main pillars until now: support for Ukraine and sanctions. European leaders have tried to shape the negotiations by influencing Donald Trump’s position, but those efforts are growing less effective. Europe also fears Trump is more interested in business deals with Moscow than in security issues.
In any direct talks, Putin could be offered two options for ending the war, Rachman writes: freezing the conflict along the front line in exchange for a guarantee that Ukraine will not join NATO, or ceding all of the Donbas to Moscow’s control, after which Kyiv could join the alliance.
Meanwhile, relations between Kyiv and Washington are going through a new crisis, triggered by an energy crisis and Trump’s push to lower diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections to Congress.
Trump has repeatedly urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries and declare an energy truce. After diplomatic failure, he struck a deal with Moscow on diesel supplies. Volodymyr Zelensky said the United States had “chosen the side” of Russia. Trump responded that it was easier for him to reach an agreement with Putin than with Zelensky, adding that Ukraine needs to hold elections.
Relations between the two leaders are at their “lowest point” since the clash in the Oval Office in 2025, the WSJ writes. The latest exchange took place a day earlier: Trump accused Zelensky of not wanting to end the war, while Zelensky said Ukraine is being pressured to capitulate.
Amid this, U.S. Vice President JD Vance has spoken out against Ukraine joining NATO: “We don’t have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They’re not in NATO. I don’t think that they should be in NATO,” he said. Vance also refused to call Kyiv an ally of Washington, saying they have “divergent interests from time to time.”

high_priority_articles.title: Does Trump’s 60-day tariff waiver really give relief to India? What it means for US trade deal & oil prices - The Times of India
high_priority_articles.summary: Does Trump’s 60-day tariff waiver really give relief to India? What it means for US trade deal & oil prices  The Times of IndiaOil Futures Pull Back as U.S. Waives Some Russia Sanctions  WSJTrump’s Russian oil waiver may boost India’s winter supplies, but crude prices unlikely to fall  ThePrintRubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions  ReutersOpinion | Great 'Exceptions': How The Oil India Was Attacked For Is The Oil Trump Now Seeks&...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
What does US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on countries buying oil from Moscow really mean for India? The US decision to waive the proposed sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 is clearly aimed at securing relief for its own country.
The development comes amid America’s shifting approach to Russian energy. In a separate deal, Russia agreed to release more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel for the US and global markets, with further supplies proposed for subsequent months.
While the US-Russia diesel deal primarily focused on the bilateral US-Russia relations, the tariff waiver is mostly directed to India and China. The threatened 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas were due to take effect 30 days after the legislation’s approval on September 18.
Also Read | 
The return of Middle East oil: Has Iran lost control of Strait of Hormuz & why are crude prices still up?
What Trump has done
Trump invoked Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to issue the waiver. He certified that it was in the national interest of the US.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act," Trump said.
The waiver applies to duties under Sections 112 and 113, which authorised tariffs of up to 500% on goods that are imported from Russia and up to 100% on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas. India and China were among the countries potentially covered by the latter provision.
Trump's sanctions and tariff waiver explained
But, Natalia Katona, Commodity Analyst sees the move as less of a gift to Moscow than an attempt to keep a lid on oil prices.
“Russian crude continued to find buyers despite the tariff threat, effectively the entire November loading programme of Russian export grades has been sold off even though it could’ve been subjected to tariffs,” she tells TOI.
“Enforcing the Lindsey Graham Act would risk disrupting future Russian crude flows and pushing Brent above its current level of around $110 a barrel. With US elections approaching in early November, my reading is that Trump wants to avoid another oil-price shock at all costs,” she says.
What it means for India
For India, the immediate relief is for its crude supply basket and exporters. If India decided to give up Russian crude oil, its single largest supplier would have gone off the table, with no easy replacement amid Middle East tensions. If it continued to buy Russian crude, then the 100% tariffs would have weighed on its exports to the US.
Russian oil supplies to India hit a record high earlier this year when the closure of Strait of Hormuz limited the Middle East crude supplies.
But recently, buying patterns have made a notable shift to the Middle East as supplies through the Strait of Hormuz ease and China begins competing for the same Russian barrels, driving up the cost of oil from Moscow.
Pankaj Srivastava, Senior Vice President, Commodity Market - Oil at Rystad Energy is of the view that India was strategically prepared for the Graham bill, with crude supply from the Middle East rising significantly to approximately 2.5 million bpd in September, while Russian imports declined to around 1.5 million bpd.
The increase in Middle Eastern supply was supported by the continued operation of multiple logistics channels, including the Strait of Hormuz, dark fleet movements, ship-to-ship transfers, alternative Red Sea and Suez Canal routes, and the East-West Pipeline.
“As a result, Middle Eastern crude exports increased to nearly 15 million barrels per day in September, strengthening India's import availability. At the same time, higher insurance and freight costs associated with Black Sea exports, following recent attacks in the region, reduced the competitiveness of Russian crude,” Pankaj Srivastava tells TOI.
According to the expert, with ongoing refinery expansions and strong diesel crack margins supporting exports, the waiver further improves feedstock security for Indian refiners.
“This development is also constructive for global distillate markets and could provide additional support to diesel and jet fuel balances in the US and Europe,” he says.
In addition, Abu Dhabi National Oil Company's decision to align Murban crude pricing with Dubai Platts from 1 November is expected to enhance pricing transparency and improve procurement flexibility for Asian refiners.
“Overall, the combination of the Russian waiver, increased Middle Eastern supply, the UAE's evolving position within OPEC, and the Murban pricing changes is positive for Indian refiners, strengthening their potential to increase diesel and jet fuel exports and generate economic benefits,” he adds.
The caveat
One very important point that is worth noting is that this waiver is for a 60-day period. This is clearly indicative that any relief from sanctions for Russia, and tariffs for countries like India is at best temporary as of now.
A day after suspending sanctions and tariffs linked to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he had not yet made a final decision on the issue. Friday's executive order did not specify the duration of the waiver.
What Marco Rubio said about the waiver
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said the administration wanted additional time to assess the implications of the move.
Rubio said Trump would take up to 60 days to examine the economic consequences of the Russia-related sanctions and tariffs he had waived a day earlier.
Rubio said Trump had chosen to review the measures over a 60-day period.
"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio said.
Separately, Rubio also appeared to recognise the practical considerations behind India's continued purchases of Russian crude.
The issue has been a key subject of discussions between him and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar since the US passed the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act in September.
"You also can't unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue. So that's the complex part of having to balance all of this,” Rubio said according to PTI.
Jaishankar is understood to have explained to Rubio that Indian refineries are largely designed to process medium-sour crude, which India sources from Middle Eastern countries and Russia.
He is also understood to have pointed out the differences in the grades of oil available from other suppliers. Venezuelan crude is heavier, while US oil is lighter and would need to be blended before Indian refineries could process it.
Will crude oil become cheaper for India?
For India, however, relief from tariffs does not necessarily mean cheaper oil. In fact, even globally despite America’s diesel supply deal with Russia and the sanctions waiver, crude oil prices continue to stay near $110 per barrel.
Pankaj Srivastava says the waiver was largely anticipated and is expected to provide modest support to crude prices while easing supply-side geopolitical risks for India.
As Natalia Katona points out: Removing the threat also removes a potential deterrent for competing buyers of Russian crude.
“So far, purchasing patterns show little sign of changing. For instance, China had already secured November-loading ESPO cargoes by early September, ahead of its usual buying schedule. India’s purchases by mid-October point to Russian crude flows of more or less the same 1.8 million b/d unchanged from September,” she tells TOI.
Brent Crude Price Trends
And, the pricing story is more complicated than the headline premium suggests.
According to Katona, the Urals deliveries to India are generally priced against Dated Brent, which reflects the tight physical crude market.
“Dated Brent was trading $20/bbl above ICE Brent futures for most of October and still is $10/bbl higher, therefore a cargo priced at Dated parity can still carry a substantial premium when compared to any other futures benchmark,” she explains.
Urals has moved from a premium of around $8/bbl to Dated Brent a month ago to roughly Dated parity today, with a possibility for that differential to soften further.
“Russian suppliers are adjusting to a higher physical benchmark and elevated freight costs to keep their barrels competitive. But a falling premium is not the same as a falling oil price,” she notes.
“India may negotiate a better differential with Russian grades and will still face a higher outright bill if the benchmark itself (in this case, Dated Brent) rises. With China competing for Russian barrels and global physical supplies tightening, the waiver eases India’s tariff risk without resolving its supply problem,” she adds.
But the weather may work in India’s favour over the coming months.
In September-October, a total of 12 cargoes carrying Russian oil transited the Northern Sea Route, on their way to China.
According to Katona, these flows should gradually halt as ice takes over most of the Arctic Ocean again, lowering the availability of Urals cargoes for China through the NSR.
“Considering India is generally closer to Russia geographically (entailing a lower freight cost), from November onwards Russian sellers of grades loading in European ports (Urals, Siberian Light or Russian CPC) should have a general prevalence for Indian deliveries,” she believes.

The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement came into effect recently, providing duty-free access to Indian goods. This agreement marks India's 17th Free Trade Agreement, which reinforces its strategic position in the Indo-Pacific.
The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA), signed on April 27, came into effect on Tuesday, providing duty-free access to a range of Indian goods, including products from labour-intensive sectors such as textiles and leather.
It is the seventh trade pact to come into force in the last five years. The others are agreements with the UAE, Mauritius, the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) bloc, the UK, Oman and Australia.
Signed on April 27, 2026, the agreement follows negotiations launched in 2010, stalled in 2015 and revived in March 2025. The pact becomes India's 17th operational FTA.
According to experts, the sectors benefiting from the FTA are textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, engineering goods and auto components, gems and jewellery, agriculture and processed foods, pharmaceuticals, and other manufacturing industries.
New Zealand has committed FDI worth USD 20 billion in over 15 years.
"The FTA's provisions on duty-free access for certain inputs, bilateral cumulation, customs facilitation, and investment-promotion mechanisms may encourage deeper value-chain integration and improve investment conditions," he said.
He added that the pact has significance beyond trade, strengthening India's strategic position in the Indo-Pacific, expanding its network of FTAs with developed economies.
At a time of growing global trade uncertainty, the India-New Zealand FTA is a strong endorsement of open markets and predictable trade rules. Its target of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 sets an ambitious agenda for both countries.
What makes this FTA particularly valuable is that it goes beyond goods to cover services, investment, skills and mobility, creating fresh opportunities for Indian professionals and businesses.
With 100 per cent of Indian exports gaining duty-free access to New Zealand from day one, the agreement gives Indian exporters a significant competitive advantage. MSMEs in textiles, leather, footwear and engineering goods are particularly well placed to benefit.
Economic think tank Chintan Research Foundation (CRF India) President Shishir Priyadarshi said that at a time of growing global trade uncertainty, the India-New Zealand FTA is a strong endorsement of open markets and predictable trade rules.
"What makes this FTA particularly valuable is that it goes beyond goods to cover services, investment, skills and mobility, creating fresh opportunities for Indian professionals and businesses," he said.
Trade expert and Hi-Tech Gears Chairman Deep Kapuria said the FTA operationalisation with New Zealand completes India's preferential market access in all major countries of the Asia-Pacific region.
"New Zealand is a very open economy; India has very well crafted this trade deal by securing market access for new services such as Ayush, yoga instructors and student mobility, including post-study work visa," he said.
Bilateral trade declined by about 11 per cent to USD 1.15 billion in 2025-26 from USD 1.3 billion in the previous fiscal year. India's exports stood at USD 566.51 million, while imports were USD 589.1 million, resulting in a meagre trade deficit of USD 22.59 million for India.
Rani Singh, Indian-origin New Zealander, said the deal is an important step forward for both countries as it is not just about trade; it is about bringing the two countries closer, creating opportunities for businesses and people, and building a stronger relationship for the future.
"India now has an opportunity to build its own strong partnership with New Zealand. With duty-free access to New Zealand for all Indian export tariff lines from day one, Indian businesses can become more competitive in this market," she said.
Singh added that the benefits are not limited to goods as there is also scope for greater cooperation in education, tourism, technology, professional services and investment.
Greater opportunities for eligible skilled professionals and young people can further strengthen these connections, she said.

high_priority_articles.title: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy as he complains US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine - Euronews
high_priority_articles.summary: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy as he complains US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine  Euronews‘I don’t care how it’s done’: Trump pressures Ukraine to cut peace deal  Al JazeeraTrump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going  BBCOpinion | Trump wants to make Zelenskyy his midterms scapegoat  MS NOWTrump’s Push for Deals With Russia Powers His Frustration With Ukraine  The New York Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Trump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he wanted his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia as he complained that the United States had received "nothing back" for its support for Kyiv.
Speaking to the media in the White House, Trump said: "We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal."
"He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," he continued, seemingly referencing the pair's heated exchange during a meeting in early 2025. "He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer."
Zelenskyy and Trump have endured a volatile relationship since the US president began his second term in January last year, but it has soured further in recent weeks after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and criticised the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia's energy sector on global fuel prices.
On Tuesday, Trump - who is gearing up for key midterm elections to determine the make-up of Congress for his final two years in office - seemed to pin the blame for the ongoing war on Zelenskyy, repeatedly saying he had had the opportunity to make a deal and that the US had got nothing in return for its help "except grief, death," and "tremendous monetary loss."
"We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine; we've got nothing back. Other than high diesel," Trump added. "The American taxpayers are tired of it."
"It's time to make a deal," he said.
Zelenskyy's Oslo talks
Trump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is scheduled to travel to Russia for a meeting with Putin on Wednesday.
Following the talks in Oslo, which also involved Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Zelenskyy had appeared relatively positive, telling journalists he had recently held a constructive call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and calling for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin.
Zelenskyy also addressed reported restrictions on US intelligence sharing during a press conference with the Nordic leaders, saying he was "thankful" that "intelligence works now."
"I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," he said.
In a post on social media later in the evening, Zelenskyy added: "It was constructive because all of us want peace – Ukraine, Europe, the United States. And we will see what happens tomorrow."

high_priority_articles.title: New Zealand’s trade pact with India removes tariffs on 57% of its exports - Vinetur
high_priority_articles.summary: New Zealand’s trade pact with India removes tariffs on 57% of its exports  Vinetur
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The deal lifts India’s 33% sheepmeat duty immediately, with duty-free access rising to 82% by 2027
Tuesday, October 20, 2026
New Zealand’s free trade agreement with India took effect on Tuesday, immediately removing Indian tariffs on 57% of New Zealand exports to that market and beginning a phased reduction of steep duties on products such as wine, honey and infant formula.
New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade said the agreement entered into force on October 20, one month after Trade and Investment Minister Todd McClay and India’s High Commissioner to New Zealand, Muanpuii Saiawi, exchanged ratification documents at Parliament. The deal was signed in New Delhi on April 27 by McClay and Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal after negotiations that began in March 2025 and concluded in December of that year.
The agreement marks one of New Zealand’s fastest trade negotiations with India. McClay told Radio New Zealand that the share of New Zealand exports entering India duty-free will rise to 82% as the pact is phased in, with the next round of tariff cuts scheduled for January 1, 2027. He said the two countries finished the talks in nine months, which he described as a record for India on a comprehensive trade agreement.
The products receiving immediate tariff-free treatment include sheepmeat, wool and coal. The Ministry’s outcomes summary says India’s 33% tariff on sheepmeat was removed on day one, while more than 95% of New Zealand forestry and wood exports now enter India duty-free. Tariffs of 33% on key fish and seafood lines will be phased out over seven years, and most industrial products will become tariff-free within 10 years. Once the agreement is fully implemented, the ministry says the average tariff applied to New Zealand’s current exports to India will fall to 3%.
Agricultural access is uneven across sectors. Horticulture gains quota-based access rather than full liberalization. New Zealand became the first country to secure preferential access for apples in an Indian trade agreement. India’s 50% tariff on apples will be cut in half within a quota that McClay said in July starts at 32,500 tonnes and rises to 45,000 tonnes by year six. Kiwifruit will receive a duty-free quota starting at 6,250 tonnes and rising to 15,000 tonnes, while the 33% tariff will be cut in half for shipments above that level.
Those quotas were set above recent trade volumes. McClay said in July that apple shipments to India were up 63% from the 2024 season and that India had risen from New Zealand’s seventh-largest apple market to its fourth-largest in two years.
Wine faces a slower path. India’s 150% tariff on New Zealand wine will be reduced over 10 years, with the final rate falling to either 25% or 50% depending on the price band. The first cut took effect Tuesday. The agreement also includes a most-favored-nation provision for wine, meaning any better deal India gives another wine-producing country will automatically apply to New Zealand. That matters because the European Union has already negotiated a lower rate with India.
For the beverage industry, the tariff phase-down opens a market that has been largely closed to New Zealand wine because of price barriers. The change could lead New Zealand wineries, distributors and importers to reassess pricing and brand positioning in India against Australian and European competitors as duties fall over time, although the pace of change will depend on how quickly tariffs come down and how producers build distribution.
New Zealand Winegrowers Chief Executive Philip Gregan said in April that India represented “a significant long-term opportunity” for the country’s wine sector. The industry body said wine exports to India were slightly below NZ$300,000 in 2025, reflecting the effect of the tariff wall.
Honey exporters also gained a limited opening. The 66% tariff on manuka honey will fall by three quarters to 16.5% over five years for honey certified by New Zealand’s Ministry for Primary Industries and priced at or above US$30 a kilogram. The ministry said this is the first time India has granted preferential access for honey to any country. Recent exports averaged only 7 tonnes a year.
Dairy, which became a central political issue during the debate over the agreement, remains mostly outside the deal. New Zealand did not secure new access for milk, cheese or butter. It did obtain a seven-year phaseout of India’s 33% tariff on bulk infant formula and other dairy-based food preparations, plus a new 3,000-tonne quota for albumins with the tariff halved to 11%. The agreement also includes a fast-track arrangement that allows Indian manufacturers to import New Zealand ingredients duty-free for products they later export.
India also agreed to consult New Zealand if it offers dairy access in the future to another comparable country, and both governments will review the entire agreement one year after it entered into force.
Meat industry groups welcomed the agreement when it was signed, while warning that gains would not be immediate. Meat Industry Association Chair Nathan Guy said in April that India was a market with “significant long-term potential” but that the agreement would not bring quick results. Beef + Lamb New Zealand Chair Kate Acland said rising incomes in India were likely to increase demand for higher-quality protein.
On New Zealand’s side, the agreement eliminates tariffs on 100% of Indian goods from Tuesday. Those tariffs had been as high as 10%. The ministry said consumers and businesses in New Zealand should see lower prices on some imports from India, including textiles, fabric, machinery and electrical goods.
The deal also includes mobility and investment provisions that have drawn political scrutiny. It provides up to 1,667 temporary three-year employment entry visas a year for Indian workers, with a cap of 5,000 holders at any one time. Of those annual places, 1,467 are tied to 13 skill-shortage occupations on New Zealand’s Green List, while 200 are reserved for chefs, yoga instructors, music teachers and Ayurveda practitioners. A separate working holiday scheme will allow up to 1,000 Indians ages 18 to 30 to travel and work in New Zealand each year.
New Zealand has also committed to promote US$20 billion in private investment into India over 15 years, while India will create a New Zealand Investment Desk to support those investors. The agreement does not include investor-state dispute settlement.
Those migration and investment terms helped shape the domestic political debate in New Zealand. Parliament passed the implementing legislation in September by 93 votes to 29. New Zealand First voted against it. Foreign Minister Winston Peters, whose party opposed the legislation, called the agreement “a bad deal for New Zealand” when negotiations concluded last December, arguing that it gave too much away on immigration while delivering too little on dairy. Labour supported the legislation but raised concerns about the migration and investment chapters.
The review built into the agreement will take place after New Zealand’s election on November 7, leaving the next government to assess how the pact is working in practice.
Trade between the two countries remains modest by New Zealand’s standards. The ministry said two-way trade totaled NZ$3.68 billion in the year to June 2025. New Zealand exported NZ$1.79 billion in goods and services to India and imported NZ$1.88 billion. India was New Zealand’s 12th-largest export market and accounted for just over 1.5% of its total exports.
The largest single New Zealand export to India was not a farm product but travel services, worth NZ$948 million, which reflects spending by Indian students and visitors in New Zealand. Forestry contributed NZ$134 million, horticulture NZ$118 million, iron and steel NZ$84 million, and wool NZ$76 million.
McClay has framed the agreement as part of the government’s goal of doubling the value of New Zealand’s exports within 10 years. He told RNZ that the pact’s entry into force was “a big step” toward that target and argued that early access matters as India’s economy expands.

Background
On September 8, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) initiated countervailing duty (CVD) investigations of imports of certain linear hydraulic cylinders and parts thereof (hydraulic cylinders) from China, India, and Mexico.[1]
Currently, the preliminary determinations are due no later than November 12, 2026.
Postponement of Preliminary Determinations
Section 703(b)(1) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), requires Commerce to issue the preliminary determination in a countervailing duty investigation within 65 days after the date on which Commerce initiated the investigation. However, section 703(c)(1) of the Act permits Commerce to postpone the preliminary determination in a CVD investigation until no later than 130 days after the date on which Commerce initiated the investigation if: (A) the petitioner makes a timely request for a postponement; or
( printed page 66295)
(B) Commerce concludes that the parties concerned are cooperating, that the investigation is extraordinarily complicated, and that additional time is necessary to make a preliminary determination. Under 19 CFR 351.205(e), the petitioner must submit a request for postponement 25 days or more before the scheduled date of the preliminary determination and must state the reasons for the request. Commerce will grant the request unless it finds compelling reasons to deny the request.
On October 14, 2026, the petitioner [2]
timely requested that Commerce postpone the preliminary CVD determinations to 130 days from the date of initiation, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.205(b) and (e).[3]
The petitioner stated a postponement is warranted to provide Commerce with additional time to review and analyze questionnaire responses, and issue supplemental questionnaires prior to making preliminary CVD determinations.[4]
In accordance with 19 CFR 351.205(e), the petitioner has stated the reasons for requesting a postponement of the preliminary determinations, and Commerce finds no compelling reason to deny the request. Therefore, in accordance with section 703(c)(1)(A) of the Act, Commerce is postponing the deadline for the preliminary determinations in the CVD investigations of hydraulic cylinders from China, India, and Mexico to no later than 130 days after the date on which these investigations were initiated,
i.e.,
January 19, 2027.[5]
Pursuant to section 705(a)(1) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.210(b)(1), the deadline for the final determinations of these investigations will continue to be 75 days after the date of the preliminary determinations.
Notification to Interested Parties
This notice is issued and published pursuant to section 703(c)(2) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.205(f)(1).

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Cairo - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has asked the country's Parliament to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia after Yemen's intensified their attacks on the kingdom, targeting and oil infrastructure.
Al-Sisi stressed that it would be a defensive mission and only if the kingdom requests assistance.
"Egypt will take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect and defend it," al-Sisi said Saturday during a military graduation ceremony.
Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of Parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.
On Sunday, al-Sisi chaired a meeting of the National Defense Council, which reviewed what the Egyptian presidency described as the "grave escalations unfolding in the region" and the "unacceptable attacks" against Saudi Arabia.
The council pledged to provide "all necessary and possible forms of support to the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, and to safeguard its resources, territorial integrity, and Islamic holy sites."
Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of all the recent military conflicts in the region and has tried to de-escalate and find political solutions. For some, this is one of al-Sisi's greatest achievements.
But Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier and political and strategic analyst, told CBS News that it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments it had made to helping secure the region.
"Egypt has repeatedly pledged to support the security of the Gulf states and has issued numerous statements reaffirming this commitment," Ragheb said. "However, this is a time of war, not politics and statements. If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats."
"The Gulf states have invested billions of dollars in Egypt. Morally, it's Egypt's turn to return the favor," he said.
Parliament convened an emergency session on Sunday and was expected to approve the resolution on Tuesday, but the vote was postponed until next Monday.
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting on the resolution, saying in a statement it had not received sufficient information about "the mission's scope, costs, and risks, as well as the arrangements in place to protect Egyptian forces."
Ragheb is certain the region is heading toward a more severe escalation.
"Egypt is not going to defend the kingdom against the Houthis," he said. "The threat is much bigger than the Houthis. This includes Iran, Iraqi militias and sleeper cells within the kingdom itself."
However, he also believes Egypt will lose much of its influence in the region if it doesn't intervene.
"If you want to be a regional player, you must play a role," he said. "Otherwise, you will lose your seat at the table."
Ragheb argued that the United States' in support of Saudi Arabia created a vacuum that must be filled by others. He said Egypt should take on the Arab share of that role.
Other regional powers are also trying to fill the vacuum. In August, Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan known as the Mecca Accords.
"Even before Saudi Arabia asked for Egyptian support, the Mecca Accords was a death certificate for the idea of relying on America for any form of defense," Ragheb said.

high_priority_articles.title: India–New Zealand FTA to Take Effect on 20 October 2026 on Vijay Dashmi, Unlocking 100% Duty-Free Market Access, New Export Opportunities and USD 20 Billion Investment Potential - A2Z Taxcorp LLP
high_priority_articles.summary: India–New Zealand FTA to Take Effect on 20 October 2026 on Vijay Dashmi, Unlocking 100% Duty-Free Market Access, New Export Opportunities and USD 20 Billion Investment Potential  A2Z Taxcorp LLP
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal and New Zealand’s Minister for Trade and Investment, Hon. Todd McClay, today jointly announced through a virtual conference that the India–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) will enter into force on 20 October 2026, on the occasion of Vijay Dashmi, a day symbolising victory and new beginnings..
Speaking on the occasion, Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal said, “Ours is a winning partnership, both on and off the field. The success of this agreement will be measured by the opportunities it creates and the difference it makes to the lives of the people of New Zealand and India. For India, 100% duty-free access to the New Zealand market opens significant new opportunities for our exporters, particularly MSMEs, artisans, farmers, and women entrepreneurs. For our farmers, the agreement combines new opportunities with appropriate safeguards. The Agricultural Productivity Partnership, with action plans for apples, kiwifruit and honey, establishment of Centres of Excellence, promote better orchard management, reduce post-harvest losses, and improve agricultural productivity, supporting stronger farm incomes across the country. The agreement also aligns with the vision of our Hon’ble Prime Minister for Viksit Bharat 2047: that is a developed and prosperous India built on competitiveness, innovation, productive capacity, and inclusive prosperity when India celebrates 100 years of independence.”
New Zealand’s Minister for Trade and Investment, Hon. Todd McClay, stated, “The entry into force of India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement is a watershed moment in the relationship between our two countries. For New Zealand exporters, the FTA opens the door to 1.4 billion consumers and one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies. New Zealand’s current exports to India will benefit from tariff elimination or substantial tariff reductions. At the same time, all Indian goods will be able to enter New Zealand duty-free, creating new opportunities for Indian exporters and placing them on a level playing field with New Zealand’s other FTA partners. The success of this agreement will ultimately be measured by the opportunities it creates and the extent to which our businesses use it.”
Secretary, Department of Commerce, Shri Rajesh Agrawal, said, “FTAs are about creating a deep economic partnership between countries. As a part of the FTA, we see this partnership also driving a lot of New Zealand investment in India. All the other big economies around the Pacific have got a much deeper trade with New Zealand. This FTA opens up the opportunity that we can also be a major contributor to the bilateral trade between India and New Zealand. The job is now to translate this opportunity into actual benefits for our people. We are working with all the Industry and the associations to take this message forward to every district across the country.”
Under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, India and New Zealand have continued to deepen and expand their engagement. The FTA reflects India’s commitment to forging partnerships with developed economies that deliver market access, create employment opportunities and empower youth, women and MSMEs, in line with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047
Representatives from industries in India and New Zealand also participated in the ceremony and spoke about opportunities created by the Agreement for their respective sectors, including services, footwear, engineering and agriculture.
On the occasion, the first-ever export of a JCB machine from India to New Zealand was flagged off by the Union Minister of Commerce and Industry. Flag-offs of a range of products across the agriculture, gems and jewellery, engineering, sporting goods, footwear and leather sectors are also planned for the entry-into-force day. These initiatives reflect the confidence of Indian manufacturers and the opportunities the Agreement opens up for exporters across the country.
New Zealand has eliminated customs duties on all tariff lines covering Indian exports, removing peak tariffs of up to 10%. Textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, gems and jewellery, engineering goods, automobiles and auto components, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, agricultural products and processed foods are expected to benefit. Duty-free access for wooden logs, coking coal and metal waste and scrap will further strengthen manufacturing and MSME supply chains. The pharmaceutical and medical device industries will benefit from streamlined regulatory processes.
New Zealand has made its best services offer in any of its trade agreements to date, with market access in around 118 sectors and Most-Favoured-Nation commitments in about 139 sub-sectors. For the first time, it has also provided dedicated access in Health and Traditional Medicine Services, covering Ayurveda, Yoga and other AYUSH systems.
Indian youth and professionals will have access to a quota of 5,000 Temporary Employment Entry visas and 1,000 Working Holiday visas every year. There will be no numerical cap on Indian students, with post-study work rights of up to three years for STEM Bachelor’s and Master’s graduates and up to four years for doctoral scholars.
The Agricultural Productivity Partnership is a key component of the Agreement, extending cooperation beyond tariff concessions to bring global technology, training and best practices to Indian farmers. It includes dedicated Action Plans for kiwifruit, apples and honey, with cooperation also extending to horticulture, forestry, livestock and fisheries.
New Zealand is providing technical assistance for establishing Centres of Excellence for kiwifruit, apples and honey. Under the Kiwifruit Action Plan, Phase I sites have been identified at Pfutsero in Nagaland and Magra in Uttarakhand. Two further Centres of Excellence for apples are proposed in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, while the Honey Action Plan envisages Centres of Excellence in Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. These initiatives aim to support farmers through technology transfer, improved cultivation practices and enhanced productivity.
Representatives from Himachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Arunachal Pradesh, along with collaborating organisations from New Zealand, were present for the entry into force.
All Tariff Rate Quotas for apples, kiwifruit and Mānuka honey are formally linked to the delivery of the Action Plans, under the oversight of a Joint Agriculture Productivity Council. This links market access with farmer welfare.
New Zealand has committed to facilitate USD 20 billion of investment into India. The investment is expected to benefit agriculture, manufacturing, infrastructure and start-ups, and support innovation, entrepreneurship and employment generation under the Make in India vision.
To protect farmers, dairy producers, fisherfolk and rural communities, sensitive products such as dairy, sugar, edible oils and key agricultural commodities remain excluded from concessions. Robust Rules of Origin, a bilateral safeguard mechanism and strong anti-circumvention provisions will ensure that the benefits flow only to genuine Indian exporters.
The Agreement opens an advanced overseas market to India’s MSMEs, women-led enterprises, start-ups, artisans and first-generation entrepreneurs. Zero duty and faster customs processes will lower landed costs and widen their customer base. Structured cooperation will provide enhanced access to trade-related information and linkages with New Zealand’s SME ecosystem, with a specific focus on enterprises owned by women and youth.
New Zealand has also committed to facilitate the registration of Indian Geographical Indications, opening avenues for protection of products associated with rural artisans and traditional industries.
The India–New Zealand FTA is a people-centric and inclusive partnership, anchored in the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 and the leadership of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. It seeks to empower farmers, MSMEs, women-led enterprises, entrepreneurs, artisans, youth and professionals.
Negotiations were launched on 16 March 2025 and concluded on 22 December 2025, within nine months. The Agreement was signed on 27 April 2026. It supports the India–New Zealand Strategic Partnership: Roadmap to 2030, which sets an aspirational goal of doubling bilateral trade in goods and services to NZ$7 billion (₹35,000 crore) by 2030.

high_priority_articles.title: European steel and downstream industries call for comprehensive EU CBAM expansion - SteelOrbis
high_priority_articles.summary: European steel and downstream industries call for comprehensive EU CBAM expansion  SteelOrbis
high_priority_articles.full_text:
European industry representatives and trade unions have issued a joint statement calling on the European Parliament, Council of the EU and European Commission to agree on the broadest possible extension of the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to downstream products during ongoing trilogue negotiations.
The signatories include the European Federation of Steel, Tubes and Metals Distribution & Trade (EUROMETAL), Electromechanics Synergy Network, European Steel Tube Association (ESTA), European Non-Integrated Wire Rod Processors Association (EUNIRPA), European Steel Association (EUROFER), European Federation of National Forging Associations (EUROFORGE), European Confederation of Associations of Manufacturers of Insulated Wires and Cables (Europacable), European Aluminium, European Federation of Steel Wire Rope Industries (EWRIS), Federation of the European Cookware, Cutlery and Housewares Industries (FEC), Metal Packaging Europe, Steel for Packaging Europe and industriAll European Trade Union.
EU ETS free allowance phaseout raises concerns over carbon leakage
According to the statement, extending CBAM coverage is necessary to protect European industrial value chains, investments and employment against carbon leakage and competition from imported products that are not subject to equivalent carbon costs.
The signatories warned that European manufacturers face increasing carbon costs throughout steel- and aluminum-intensive value chains, while competing finished and semi-finished products imported from third countries may continue to enter the EU market without bearing comparable costs.
These risks will become more pronounced as free emissions allowances under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) are gradually phased out. Broader CBAM coverage would help address differences in carbon costs between European manufacturers and competing imports.
Downstream steel and aluminum sectors face import competition
Several downstream sectors exposed to competition from carbon-intensive imports include energy, automotive and other mobility applications, machinery, construction, packaging, clean technologies and defense. Other affected sectors include household appliances, cookware, cutlery, catering equipment, hand tools and other metal products.
Products included within CBAM's scope would benefit from more balanced competitive conditions, while products excluded from the mechanism could face greater risks of import substitution and production relocation to countries with lower carbon costs. The organizations therefore called on EU policymakers to build on the positions adopted by the European Parliament and Council and ensure comprehensive coverage of downstream products in the final agreement. They also urged the EU institutions to prioritize European industrial production, investment and employment, emphasizing their importance for the region's economic security, industrial competitiveness and climate transition.

high_priority_articles.title: The Ministry of Economy should step up its efforts with the EU to delay the CBAM — EBA - ЭкоПолитика
high_priority_articles.summary: The Ministry of Economy should step up its efforts with the EU to delay the CBAM — EBA  ЭкоПолитика
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The Ministry of Economy and Environment must step up its cooperation with the European Commission and EU Member States so that Ukraine can finally benefit from special conditions for the application of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
The European Business Association addressed the ministry with this appeal.
Enormous losses for the state and pressure on businesses
Data from the GMK Centre indicates that, between 2026 and 2030, losses to Ukrainian exports due to the impact of the mechanism could ‘skyrocket’ from $372 million to $1.754 billion.
Ukraine’s GDP losses will be many times higher. Their potential total by 2030 could reach $7,248 billion.
At the same time, as the cost of SVAM certificates rises, so too will the burden on businesses. And the price is not stable — in the third quarter it stood at €82.32, which is 10 per cent higher than in the second quarter.
The scope of the mechanism is not fixed either — the list of products subject to the carbon ‘duty’ may include hundreds of derivative goods with a high steel and aluminium content.
Key areas of work
In its statement, the EBA calls on the Ministry of Economy to focus on two areas of work:
Strategic. This involves the development of a special regime for Ukraine, as provided for in Regulation (EU) 2023/956. It differs for the two periods:
- during the period of martial law — a deferral of payments for embedded emissions arising from imports into the EU. Subsequent settlement of financial obligations under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) must take place through verified decarbonisation and environmental modernisation projects;
- From the end of martial law until integration with the European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS), revenues from the Domestic Emissions Trading Scheme (SVA) should be accumulated in a special fund. The funds in this scheme should be used to finance decarbonisation projects.
EVA proposes introducing regular joint consultations between the business community and the Ministry of Economy. The business community believes this will help to jointly formulate proposals for Ukraine’s negotiating position.
The practical component involves the following activities:
- a review of the default emission factors for Ukrainian steel and cement products;
- developing mechanisms for verifying actual emissions in wartime;
- exemption of Ukrainian cement and cement clinker from the accounting of indirect emissions.
"This approach will make it possible to minimise the negative impact of the CBAM on Ukrainian industry, preserve enterprises’ export opportunities and investment potential, whilst at the same time creating the conditions for decarbonisation and Ukraine’s gradual integration into the European climate system," the Association emphasised.

Πηγή Φωτογραφίας: AP Photo//Rubio in Samarkand: Trump’s Russia Sanctions U-Turn Reshapes the US–China–Russia Power Game
Samarkand Becomes a Strategic Battleground for Three Major Powers
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, highlights Central Asia’s growing geopolitical importance as a region positioned between Russia, China and the strategic trade and energy corridors of Eurasia.
Washington is seeking to expand its economic and strategic presence through investment, commercial agreements and access to American financing.
However, the diplomatic initiative comes at a time when President Donald Trump’s administration has altered its approach to certain sanctions measures targeting Russia.
The suspension of new restrictions, combined with Washington’s agreement to import Russian diesel, has raised questions about the durability and predictability of American economic pressure.
For Central Asian governments, this development represents more than uncertainty.
It could become an additional bargaining advantage.
The region possesses natural resources, strategic infrastructure and trade routes that are increasingly important to all three major powers.
The central question is whether Washington can secure economic and strategic cooperation without weakening the mechanisms it has established to pressure Moscow.
More Than 100 American Companies Accompany Rubio
Marco Rubio arrived in Samarkand on Sunday, October 18, for his first visit to Central Asia as US secretary of state.
The American delegation includes representatives of more than 100 companies, underscoring the economic importance of the initiative.
Critical minerals, rare earth elements, energy resources, trade corridors and financing for major investment projects are at the center of the agenda.
Washington’s strategy extends beyond strengthening diplomatic relations.
Its objective is to establish economic partnerships that provide Central Asian countries with alternatives to Russian and Chinese influence.
Central Asia holds significant reserves of uranium, tungsten and other raw materials essential to defense manufacturing, advanced technology and the energy transition.
For the United States, securing access to these resources is both an economic competitiveness issue and a national security priority.
Two Days Before the Summit, Trump Changes the Equation
The American delegation arrives following a significant decision by the White House.
On October 16, Donald Trump issued an executive order suspending the implementation of provisions in new sanctions legislation he had signed the previous month.
The legislation, associated with an initiative by Senators Lindsey Graham and Richard Blumenthal, authorized substantial tariffs against countries purchasing Russian energy or facilitating sanctions evasion.
According to the analysis underlying the debate, the proposed tariffs could reach 100%.
Kazakhstan was among the countries potentially exposed to the new measures.
The suspension followed the October 9 agreement concerning imports of Russian diesel into the United States.
Together, these decisions have created a different political environment.
Sanctions remain an instrument of American foreign policy, but the recent suspension demonstrates that the implementation of certain new measures can change according to Washington’s political and economic priorities.
That is precisely what Central Asian governments are watching.
Central Asia: A Transit Route Into Russia’s War Economy
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Central Asian trade routes have become increasingly important for shipments of goods entering the Russian market.
Some of these products appear on Western high-priority lists because they can serve both civilian and military purposes.
They include electronic components, microchips, machine tools and parts potentially used in unmanned systems.
According to research cited by Eurasianet, Kazakhstan’s exports to Russia of certain high-priority dual-use products increased by more than 400% in 2022.
These flows declined significantly over the following two years as the risk of secondary sanctions increased.
However, the same research identified renewed growth in certain trade flows through Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan in 2025.
Importantly, the findings did not establish systematic involvement by Kazakhstan’s government in circumventing sanctions.
Geographical proximity to Russia, established commercial networks and Kazakhstan’s membership in the Eurasian Economic Union create conditions in which export controls are particularly difficult to enforce.
The challenge therefore concerns not only government policy but also the behavior of private companies and intermediary trading networks.
Why Secondary Sanctions Depend on Credibility
Secondary sanctions allow the United States to exert pressure on companies and financial institutions in third countries that conduct business with sanctioned entities.
Their effectiveness does not depend exclusively on penalties already imposed.
It also depends on how businesses assess the likelihood of future enforcement.
A company considering the export of machine tools to a Russian buyer must evaluate not only existing legislation but also the risk of future investigations and penalties.
The more consistent and predictable enforcement appears, the stronger the incentive to comply.
Conversely, when governments observe that significant provisions can be suspended or become part of political negotiations, their calculations change.
This does not mean companies are released from existing legal obligations.
It means uncertainty over future enforcement acquires economic and diplomatic value.
The credibility of sanctions is therefore not merely a legal matter.
It is also a question of expectations.
Kazakhstan: A Case Study in Multivector Foreign Policy
Kazakhstan illustrates how Central Asian governments seek to maintain partnerships with competing major powers.
To the United States, it offers access to critical minerals, investment opportunities and commercial agreements.
With Russia, it maintains substantial economic, energy and institutional ties.
To China, it offers access to overland trade corridors and alternative transportation routes connecting Asia with Europe.
This multivector foreign policy is not new.
However, intensifying competition between Washington, Moscow and Beijing has increased its strategic significance.
Kazakhstan can attract American investment without severing its economic relationships with Russia.
It can also develop cooperation with China without excluding Western financing and technology.
For Astana, the challenge is to preserve these relationships without becoming exposed to sanctions or creating dependencies that restrict its strategic autonomy.
The $25 Billion Investment Push and the Battle for Critical Minerals
Washington’s engagement with Central Asia has already acquired a substantial economic dimension.
At the White House summit with Central Asian leaders in November 2025, agreements worth approximately $25 billion were announced.
Among them was a tungsten project in Kazakhstan valued at approximately $1.1 billion.
Tungsten is particularly important for industrial and defense applications, while secure supply chains have become an increasingly important American priority.
Washington is also interested in uranium and rare earth elements.
Developing new investment projects could provide regional governments with additional financing and export opportunities.
At the same time, American businesses are seeking access to markets where Russia and China maintain established positions.
The unresolved question is whether these commercial agreements will include specific commitments concerning export controls and sanctions compliance.

Despite growing American interest, Russia continues to play a significant role in Kazakhstan’s energy strategy.
Russia’s state nuclear corporation, Rosatom, has secured the contract to construct the country’s first nuclear power plant.
Under the reported terms of the arrangement, Russia is expected to finance approximately 85% of the project.
The agreement demonstrates the depth of the economic relationship between Astana and Moscow.
Large energy projects establish long-term technological, financial and operational partnerships.
Consequently, a stronger American presence does not automatically translate into diminished Russian influence.
Kazakhstan is seeking to develop relationships with multiple partners rather than committing itself exclusively to one geopolitical bloc.
The Russian Oil Corridor and the Importance of Sanctions Exemptions
Kazakhstan’s reliance on transportation routes through Russia is another critical factor.
Approximately 80% of the country’s oil exports reach international markets through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which terminates on the Black Sea.

India Becomes World's Second-Largest Solar Market
India overtook the US to become the world's second-largest solar market in 2025, adding nearly 50 GW, with analysts forecasting continued expansion of 526 GW.
Global solar supply chains are shifting toward protectionism and industrial policies designed to support domestic manufacturing, according to an interview with pv magazine featuring Laura Sartore, CEO of Italian solar machinery and production line specialist Ecoprogetti. Sartore told the publication that every major supply chain worldwide except China is moving toward some form of protectionism and price floors, with the United States among the most prominent examples.
According to Sartore, the US market demonstrates that minimum price thresholds, even when set above the prices charged by Chinese manufacturers, do not necessarily slow demand. She indicated that the sector continues to grow despite higher component costs, supported by the development of a domestic supply chain. In China, prices are also rising gradually across the supply chain after government efforts to curb overcapacity, a trend that was expected to continue into 2025. Sartore said this reflects a growing focus on the economic viability of manufacturing in a market where solar technology has already established its competitiveness against other energy sources.
Sartore identified India as one of the most compelling examples of industrial policy in the solar sector. The Indian government is progressively expanding protectionist measures and domestic manufacturing requirements beyond modules to include cells, wafers and ingots, aiming to reduce dependence on Chinese imports and strengthen local production capacity. Sartore said India has the most serious industrial policy, having observed Europe's mistakes and continuing to monitor developments in the United States, and she highlighted the clear industrial strategy of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
A key element of that strategy is industry consolidation. Production capacity exceeding domestic demand is not necessarily seen as a problem and can instead encourage mergers and direct investment toward underdeveloped segments of the supply chain. Sartore said the era of small factories with 200-500 MW of capacity is over and that multi-gigawatt-scale facilities are now emerging, which she described as the only way forward for a continent-sized nation like India. This consolidation is helping create larger, more financially robust manufacturers able to invest not only in cell and module production but also in materials and components such as glass, encapsulants, backsheets and junction boxes.
According to Sartore, India now has the most comprehensive solar manufacturing supply chain outside China, though domestic polysilicon production remains underdeveloped. She explained that beyond raw material extraction, polysilicon production requires specialized technological expertise, capital-intensive facilities and competitive access to energy, capabilities she said are currently lacking and must be developed. She also stressed that India must aim for high environmental standards and low-emission processes from the outset rather than simply replicating capacity without prioritizing emissions, noting that these requirements could lengthen the timeline for building a domestic supply chain.
While India and the United States focus on large-scale factories and highly integrated supply chains, Sartore advocates a different approach for Europe. She argues that Europe's industrial model cannot be assessed by the same criteria applied in the United States or Asia, since the continent's manufacturing sector has historically been built around small and medium-sized enterprises, industrial clusters and networks of specialized manufacturers. She pointed to Italy and Germany, where industries have achieved international leadership through networks of relatively small but highly competitive companies, and said Europe's multi-factory, network-based model should not be abandoned.
This does not mean small module assembly lines can remain competitive regardless of capacity. Sartore said manufacturers need a minimum production scale and adequate investment in technology and automation to justify capital expenditure and maintain competitive costs, citing 800 MW to 1 GW as the minimum threshold for a sustainable investment. She identified 1 GW to 3 GW as offering an optimal balance between economies of scale, financial viability and operational complexity, typically corresponding to companies with annual revenue of EUR100 million to EUR200 million and roughly 150 to 300 employees.
Sartore noted that operating costs, particularly raw material procurement, present a challenge beyond initial capital investment. While increasing capacity initially reduces unit production costs, there is a point beyond which the financial burden of running a larger facility offsets those savings. She said that in the European context the 1 GW to 3 GW range captures economies of scale, while beyond 3 GW additional management costs and financial charges weigh on the bottom line without necessarily lowering raw material procurement costs. For a 5 GW factory, working capital requirements can become significant, requiring substantial credit lines, bank guarantees and careful financial planning, and larger facilities also face greater financial exposure if demand falls short of capacity.
Sartore explained that in Europe, without supply chain integration, purchasing 5 GW worth of raw materials would require structured bank collateral, with high costs for credit guarantees and interest on cash flow weighing on the purchase price and potentially making the resulting module no more cost-effective than one from a smaller manufacturer. She said a larger factory therefore does not necessarily have lower production costs than a medium-sized facility once financing expenses and operating overheads are considered, and that a more moderate scale can help medium-sized European manufacturers limit financial exposure and manage working capital.
Production capacity should also reflect market demand, according to Sartore. Europe's solar market is more fragmented than other major international markets, with projects generally smaller than gigawatt-scale installations and manufacturers required to handle a wider range of order sizes. European projects often range from a few megawatts to several tens of megawatts, while installations approaching or exceeding 1 GW remain relatively rare. Sartore said this supports a network of manufacturers able to adapt production to individual customer requirements, adding that Europe is unlikely to see many gigawatt-scale solar plant projects and that diverse requirements and local conditions make numerous medium-to-large plants more likely than many mega-installations. Production flexibility therefore becomes a key competitive factor alongside manufacturing costs and supply chain capabilities.
The dynamics shaping global photovoltaic supply chains, including modules, inverters and battery energy storage systems, are scheduled to be discussed during a session titled Decoding solar supply chains at the NetZero event in Milan on Oct. 21.

high_priority_articles.summary: How the Iran war is ruining Saudi Arabia’s plans  VoxEverything is going wrong for Muhammad bin Salman  The EconomistSaudi Arabia’s Military Limitations Are Being Exposed by Houthi Attacks  WSJWhy the Houthis Are So Hard to Defeat  Bloomberg.comHow Saudi Arabia Created the Yemen It Fears  The National Interest
high_priority_articles.full_text:
As the US-Iran war drags on, the damage is being felt regionally: Saudi Arabia experienced the worst attack in over a decade earlier this month, when Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militia struck an airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. The strike killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others.
Saudi Arabia responded with missile attacks on Yemen, striking oil facilities, and the Houthis have launched more strikes of their own, targeting Saudi oil infrastructure.
The dueling strikes are the latest development in a decade-plus of conflict between Saudi and the Houthis, a political and military group that controls part of northern Yemen, which had been on pause until earlier this year after a 2022 ceasefire. But the Iran war, and Houthi affiliation with Iran’s network of proxy groups, mean the current violence has far-reaching implications for the US, Israel, and the global energy economy.
It also threatens more than just Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil industry: As Gregg Carlstrom, a Middle East correspondent for The Economist, explains, the attacks cut at the heart of the country’s project to evolve into a destination for foreign investment, travel, tourism, and more. On Monday, the country’s upcoming Future Investment Initiative was postponed until 2027.
Carlstrom, who is based in Riyadh, spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram how the attack has been received inside Saudi Arabia, why it comes at an especially bad time for the country, and how President Donald Trump might — or might not — get more involved.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Can you help us understand how the Houthis have such a presence in the country right now? Are they infiltrating the country? Are they already there?
They’re shooting from outside the country. They’re shooting from Yemen. The Houthis are a group that’s been around for a few decades. They were originally a local insurgency in Yemen that was fighting against the Yemeni government. They originate from the northern part of Yemen, but they were able to gain control of large parts of that country from 2014 onwards. Ali Abdullah Saleh, the longtime dictator of Yemen, was overthrown during the Arab Spring and the Houthis were able to seize a large chunk of territory.
They are effectively in control of most of the population centers in Yemen. They have received increasing support from Iran, which has provided them with weapons, with money, with know-how, and technical expertise. And they have used that to build an arsenal of drones and missiles, which they are using now to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia.
And was there a particular reason they targeted the airport in Riyadh? Were they trying to send a message here?
If you listen to the messaging from the Houthis, they are trying to describe this as almost a like-for-like campaign, where you’ve had years in which the Saudi-led coalition, which invaded Yemen in 2015, has been imposing a blockade of Yemeni airspace, has been restricting flights in and out of that country.
And so the Houthis describe this publicly as being a retaliation in kind, but I think they’ve also just figured out that attacks on airports are a very effective way to cause economic disruption in Saudi Arabia. You prevent not just people from flying in and out but also, as we’ve seen disruptions to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, a lot of cargo that these countries depend on for daily needs are coming in by air instead.
Carrying out these sorts of attacks, shutting down the airport in a capital city, is a very effective way for the Houthis to impose economic pain on the Saudis.
And I guess on some level it makes the country feel insecure. How is that making Saudi Arabia’s leader feel right now? What’s his response been?
It comes at a very difficult time for the Saudi leadership because they are supposed to be hosting a number of events this month where Saudi will be playing a role on the world stage.
There’s something called the World Petroleum Congress that is taking place this week [October 11–15], which is normally a big event that draws executives from top oil and gas companies. Many of them canceled their participation because of the attacks on the airport.
Then they are supposed to be hosting the [now-postponed] Future Investment Initiative, which is something often known outside Saudi Arabia as “Davos in the Desert.” It’s the sort of flagship investment conference that takes place here every year. It draws a who’s who of global finance.
For a country that is trying to diversify its economy, a country that is trying to attract foreign investment and make itself into a hub for finance and travel and tourism, these sorts of attacks are very detrimental to those goals.
And this is coming as Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the rest of the leadership in the country is really trying to establish Saudi Arabia as the premier economic hub in the region. The stakes are really high for him right now?
They are. And just about everything that they are trying to do is being disrupted by what’s happened over the past few weeks.
If you look at travel, for example, the Public Investment Fund, which is the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, last year launched a new airline, Riyadh Air, which they are hoping will eventually compete with Emirates or Qatar Airways, the really big carriers in the Gulf.
That airline was just getting into regular operations this summer where they were growing their fleet, they were growing their network of destinations. And then suddenly this happens and their home base in Riyadh is shut down. They have moved some of their planes out of Riyadh to other airports to keep them safe from Houthi attacks. Obviously, it’s very disruptive for trying to build an air carrier.
In Riyadh itself, the financial district — this sort of long-planned attempt to set up a banking hub that might rival the one in Dubai — had just started to get going over the past couple of years, when you had banks and other financial services firms moving in there. Everybody who works there has now been told to work remotely for the foreseeable future because there is a concern about possible Houthi attacks against skyscrapers and the financial district.
Everything they are trying to do, from finance to travel to trade, all of it is being disrupted and threatened by what’s happening in Yemen.
What options does he have to reassure investors and the world really that he can protect the country and maybe especially his airport, where a bunch of the investment is focused?
The airport, I think, is going to be difficult to reassure people about. You can install additional air defenses there. You can move more batteries and more interceptors there, but at the end of the day, no air defense system is hermetic. There’s no 100 percent guarantee that you’re going to shoot down every incoming projectile.
As long as there is this ongoing war between the Houthis and Yemen and the Saudis, I think people might have ongoing concerns about the airport. You have to resolve that underlying issue to give people confidence.
Now, how do you try to resolve that? If you’re Saudi Arabia right now, you have two bad options. One is you keep fighting. You try to militarily defeat the Houthis or at least force them to accept a renewed ceasefire.
The other option is you cut a deal. You try to offer the Houthis some concessions that might encourage them to go back to the ceasefire. That’s going to be very costly for Saudi Arabia. I’ve heard that the Houthis are demanding probably billions of dollars of financial concessions where they would want the Saudis to offer some money for reconstruction and to pay the salaries of Yemeni civil servants working in Houthi-controlled areas.
If you are the Saudi leadership right now, neither one is really a good option.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has a pretty strong relationship with the president of the United States, who’s very sympathetic to Saudi Arabia and Saudi investment. Has he appealed to President Trump for help here yet?
He has. He’s done so repeatedly over the past month or so, asking not just for support with the Saudi campaign in Yemen, but for America to carry out its own airstrikes in Yemen. And the response so far from Donald Trump has been to refuse that.
For the US to get involved in a bigger way, there are some practical constraints at the moment where a lot of American military assets are tied up in the Strait of Hormuz trying to keep that open, keep oil flowing through the Strait. And so the response from Trump has been disappointing for the Saudi Crown prince. The US is providing intelligence support. It’s helping on that front, but it is not directly getting involved in the war in Yemen.
