Bank of America Maintains October Fed Rate Hike Forecast Ahead of October 28 Decision
Bank of America analysts reiterated their expectation that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in October, according to Investing.com. The bank made the case in a note issued Monday, ahead of the central bank's next rate decision, which is scheduled for Wednesday, October 28.
Market pricing currently assigns a 20% probability to a rate increase at that meeting, the bank noted. Bank of America nonetheless maintained its forecast, citing September inflation data as strengthening the argument for an October move.
The bank observed that the inflation picture has deteriorated since the September meeting. It also projected that core PCE could plausibly finish the year at 3.4% year over year, pointing to the risk that an energy shock gets passed through amid a booming nominal economy.
Bank of America highlighted that most of the Federal Open Market Committee supported two rate hikes this year. On that basis, it questioned why the committee would forgo the second increase in October while preserving the option for a third in December.
The bank concluded that the decision ultimately depends on the character of Chair Walsh. It described its conviction as low regarding whether he is serious about bringing a sea change to the Fed, but said it was giving him the benefit of the doubt by retaining its October hike forecast.

Oil Holds Its Risk Premium as Houthi Strikes Offset Russia Relief
Crude markets start the week with uncertainty after the US softened its stance on buying Russian oil, while the attack on Saudi’s energy facilities last weekend drew wider concern.
Brent: Saudi Supply in the Crosshairs
Yemen’s Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for multiple attacks over the weekend, including attacks on Saudi energy and airport infrastructure and the Shaybah oilfield. According to ING, the market remains at risk premium due to the heightened war risk.
Russian supplies are also coming under increased pressure. A series of drone attacks by Ukraine over the weekend set fire to an oil terminal and a nearby depot in St. Petersburg. The terminal, according to Kpler, exports approximately 120,000 bpd of refined petroleum products.
However, the other way on the scale is President Trump’s executive order from Friday, which removed sanctions and tariffs relating to Russia, including penalties on countries buying Russian energy.
WTI: Inventories Back in Focus
Inventories are likely back in focus for WTI after a week of solid gains last week. The Cushing stock build last week was smaller than expected and markets will now look toward EIA inventory data for further insight.
A Reuters poll showed crude and products stockpiles are expected to have dropped last week. Data shows US stockpiles have been declining over the last couple of weeks, which keeps the focus on domestic supply ahead of the EIA’s report this week. The Nov WTI contract expires on Tuesday.
Natural Gas: Mild Weather Versus Record LNG Pull
On Monday, expectations for milder weather cut forecasts for heating demand, which countered bullish factors like small storage builds, lower production and LNG demand. On average, LNG feedgas has been at 18.1 bcfd. Lower 48 production averaged 111.3 bcfd.
Two opposing factors influenced the gas and LNG market this week. LNG feedgas hit a new high at 20.7 bcfd. Meanwhile, Columbia Gas restored 1.9mn Dth/d of capacity, bringing supply back to Appalachia. While that has increased supply in the US, the attack on ships in the Middle East has limited global LNG supply, making it more difficult for Europe to restock for the winter.
Natural Gas Technical Analysis: NG Slips Below $3.03 as $2.97 Support Comes Into Focus
Natural gas is currently trading at around $3.01/MMBtu, and what’s notable is the sustained selling following last week’s triangle breakdown. The most recent bounce ended at $3.09 and price has fallen below the previous support of $3.03 and $3.05. The moving averages are both falling, and the faster moving average is still below the slower moving average, which keeps the short-term trend bearish.
The first major support I’m looking at is at $2.97. If that support is breached, then $2.91 would be the next support and that would also be a breakdown of the previous uptrend that started from the early October lows. If that happens, then $2.87 would be the next support.
Resistance is at $3.03, $3.09 and $3.15. The RSI is at 34, and still bearish. A recovery above $3.03 would also negate the bearish case, and so would a move above $3.09. I would also add that if $3.09 is broken, then a more serious move to the upside could take place. From there a return to $3.15 would still be in the realm of possibility.
WTI Technical Analysis: USOIL Holds $98.09 as $99.72 Remains the Key Breakout Test
WTI crude is at $98.67 on the 1 hour chart. On the upward channel from mid-October, the price has tested lower levels and been defended by the lower level of the channel. Twice the price has tried to break out at $99.72 and has formed a double top with the last high from October 10th. For now, the price is above both moving averages.
$99.72 is the first major resistance. If this breaks, $100.86, and the channel upper level, would be the next target. $98.09 and the lower channel line would provide support, followed by $97.65. Even lower $96.73 and $95.34 would provide support.
RSI is at 55 and falling, signaling that a drop may occur, but the lower level of the channel continues to be defended, so a drop may be short-lived.
If $98.09 and the channel lower level is defended, I would view the outlook as slightly bullish. A break of $99.72 would provide a better outlook. A close below $96.73 would flatten the channel.
Brent Technical Analysis: UKOIL Holds $109.97 as $111.07 Comes Into Focus
Brent is trading at $109.92 as of the 1-hour chart. What I find important is how strongly the breakout from the contracting triangle held. The previous resistance at $107.00 to $107.57, which rejected price 3 times, has since turned to support. A rising trendline is also supporting the lows, while both moving averages are still far from price and are pointing up.
The first resistance I am looking at is $111.07, where the last leg of the move higher stopped. Breaking through that would bring $112.08 into play. Supporting the move lower would be the $109.97 pivot level, then the rising trendline and $108.83. Further down, the $108.14 level and the previous breakout of $107.57 would come into play.
RSI is at 59, and is headed lower, and has slipped just below the signal line at 62. That suggests bullish momentum and a mild uptrend is still in place. However, that may change if price breaks below $108.83.
I am leaning slightly bullish, and would expect $108.83 to act as support. I would also expect $111.07 to be a stiff resistance, and possibly a breakout level to the upside. A close below $107.57 would bring the contracting triangle into question.

Jammu and Kashmir's challenging terrain is steadily yielding to a new era of connectivity. The Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla Rail Link has connected the valley to India's rail network. Its centrepiece, the Chenab Bridge, stands as the world's highest railway arch bridge. Expanded Vande Bharat services are improving passenger mobility. New freight terminals are carrying Kashmiri apples, saffron and handicrafts to national markets, opening opportunities for farmers and businesses. On land, the Sonamarg and Zojila tunnels promise year-round passage into Ladakh. In the air, Srinagar's expanding airport is complemented by nascent hubs at Udhampur and Kishtwar. Together, these advances are drawing Kashmir's produce, trade and tourism firmly into the national mainstream.
A Region Reconnected
Jammu and Kashmir's mountainous terrain has long made connectivity a major infrastructure challenge. Over the years, this has been steadily changing, with a wave of infrastructure investment reshaping how the region connects with the rest of the country. The Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla Rail Link (USBRL) project is a major part of this expansion. It is one of the most challenging railway line projects undertaken in the country post-independence. Today it stands as one of India’s engineering marvels, linking the Kashmir Valley to the rest of the country by rail.
The USBRL project has also been accompanied by sustained expansion of roads, tunnels and airport infrastructure. The network now includes new train services such as the Vande Bharat Express. It also includes major road corridors and tunnels. Airport capacity is being expanded at Srinagar, with regional airports planned under UDAN, increasing passenger movement. Multimodal cargo terminals and enhanced freight services support goods movement across the region. These developments have progressively expanded all-weather connectivity infrastructure across Jammu and Kashmir.
Railways: Connecting Kashmir to the National Rail Network
Udhampur-Srinagar-Baramulla Rail Link (USBRL) National Project
The USBRL project was inaugurated in June 2025, improving connectivity infrastructure in the Himalayan region. Built at a cost of ₹43,780 crore, the USBRL project covers the districts of Udhampur, Reasi, Ramban, Srinagar, Anantnag, Pulwama, Budgam and Baramulla of Jammu and Kashmir.
The project stretches 272 kilometres through the rugged Himalayas; it includes 36 tunnels that span 119 kilometres and 943 bridges. Designed to overcome the region’s challenging terrain, it connects remote areas with the national rail network. It is opening new opportunities for mobility, trade and tourism. As part of the USBRL project, over 215 km (including a tunnel and 320 bridges) of roads have been constructed, which are useful for communities. Additionally, the USBRL project is fully electrified both in tunnels and in open stretches.
The USBRL project has made substantial socio-economic contributions to the region, with employment generation being a significant aspect of its impact. The project has generated more than 5 crore man-days of employment.
Vande Bharat Express
Vande Bharat Express, Jammu and Kashmir
The Vande Bharat Express in Jammu and Kashmir first began operations in June 2025, between Katra and Srinagar. To further enhance railway connectivity, the Srinagar-Katra Vande Bharat Express service was extended to Jammu Tawi Railway Station in April 2026.
The distance from Jammu to Srinagar is now covered in less than five hours. The trains have been augmented from 8 to 20 coaches. They are specially designed to operate in extreme weather conditions. The trains are equipped with advanced operating systems and electronics suited for high-altitude conditions.
Supporting this route is a snow removal train that moves ahead to clear the tracks, ensuring year-round services. Seismic dampers have also been installed to absorb tremors, offering a safer and smoother journey in this high-risk zone.
Engineering Marvels under the USBRL Project
The USBRL project includes several major engineering achievements, including the Chenab Rail Bridge, Anji Khad Bridge and Tunnel T50.
Chenab Rail Bridge
Under the USBRL project, the world’s highest railway arch bridge has been built over the Chenab River in the Reasi district of Jammu and Kashmir. The Chenab bridge, inaugurated in June 2025, is 1,315 m long. It has an arch span of 467 metres and rises 359 metres above the riverbed, making it higher than the Eiffel Tower. The bridge is designed to withstand strong seismic and wind forces. With Vande Bharat services running over the bridge, connectivity has significantly improved between Jammu and Kashmir.
Chenab Rail Bridge in Jammu and Kashmir
Anji Khad Bridge in Jammu and Kashmir
The Anji Khad bridge is India’s first cable-stayed railway bridge built above the Anji River gorge, a tributary of the Chenab River. The Anji Khad bridge is part of the USBRL project and was inaugurated in June 2025.
The bridge is located in the Reasi district of Jammu and Kashmir. It is supported by a single 193-metre-high tower shaped like an inverted ‘Y’, with cables supporting the bridge. The main bridge has a total length of 473.25 metres, designed for the region’s challenging terrain and seismic conditions.
Tunnel T50 in Jammu and Kashmir
Tunnel T50, inaugurated in 2024, is a 12.77-km rail tunnel linking Khari and Sumber in Jammu and Kashmir. It is India’s longest transportation tunnel, built under the USBRL project. The tunnel provides a vital rail link between the Kashmir Valley and the rest of India.
The New Austrian Tunnelling Method has been used to construct the tunnel through the challenging Himalayan geology. The tunnel engineering overcame the challenges of high-water ingress, landslides, shear zones, and jointed volcanic rocks. The tunnel features a main tube paired with a parallel escape tunnel, linked every 375 metres for safety. CCTV cameras are placed every 50 metres, which help monitor from a central control room.
Supporting Railway Infrastructure
Railway connectivity in Jammu and Kashmir is being strengthened through increased investment in supporting infrastructure and network development. The annual average budget of railways for Jammu and Kashmir has increased from ₹1,044 crore in 2009–14 to ₹1,086 crore in 2026–27.
Electrification
Indian Railways has pursued railway electrification in mission mode, with about 99.6% of the Broad Gauge (BG) network now electrified. In Jammu and Kashmir, the entire existing BG network is electrified. All new-line and multi-tracking projects are being sanctioned and built with electrification from the outset.
Station Redevelopment
Under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme, 1,340 stations have been identified for redevelopment across Indian Railways. Among them, four stations are in Jammu and Kashmir. The stations are Budgam, Jammu Tawi, Martyr Captain Tushar Mahajan (Udhampur) and Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra station.

Roads: Strengthening Surface Connectivity
Roads as a complement to Rail
In Jammu and Kashmir, road infrastructure is expanding alongside railway infrastructure. Roads remain essential for last-mile access to places outside the railway network. In August 2026, foundation stones were laid for 110 road projects covering 598.455 km under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY)-IV. Costing more than ₹1,500 crore, the projects are expected to benefit 46,972 people across the Udhampur–Kathua–Doda–Kishtwar region. The projects also include the use of waste plastics in several road packages, supporting more sustainable road construction.
Tunnel construction has also become a key component of development in the Himalayan region to ensure all-weather connectivity, improve road safety, and enhance strategic mobility.
Sonamarg Tunnel, Jammu and Kashmir
The Sonamarg tunnel project, also known as the Z-Morh, inaugurated in January 2025, is a 6.4 km bi-directional tunnel with a parallel escape tunnel of length 6.4 km and an approach road of length 5.5km. Constructed at a cost of over ₹2,700 crore, the tunnel sits at an altitude of 2634 meters above sea level. The tunnel provides all-weather connectivity between Srinagar and Sonamarg enroute to Leh. It bypasses parts of the road hit by major avalanches and landslides. It promotes tourism by transforming Sonamarg into a year-round destination, boosting winter tourism, adventure sports and local livelihoods. Along with the Zojila Tunnel, it will cut the NH-1 section of this project from 13 km to 11.98 km.
Zojila Tunnel
The Zojila Tunnel is a 13.153-kilometre-long bi-directional tunnel being constructed between Baltal and Minamarg on National Highway-1 by NHIDCL. Elevated at 2,900–3,310 metres, the ₹6,808-crore project will provide all-weather year-round road connectivity between Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. With construction beginning in October 2020, the main tunnel achieved breakthrough in June 2026.

Turkey advances mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan amid Houthi attacks
Turkey took a step toward expanding its security presence in the Gulf on Tuesday by submitting the trilateral Mecca Joint Defense Agreement to parliament for ratification, Reuters reported.
The treaty, signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, moves NATO’s second-largest army closer to a formal defense commitment to Riyadh as Saudi Arabia faces attacks by the Houthis.
Under the pact's primary clause, an armed attack on any member state is treated as an attack on all, requiring signatories to use all necessary means to eliminate threats to each other's sovereignty and territorial integrity, according to text seen by Reuters.
The agreement also establishes a framework for intelligence sharing, logistical support and defense-industry collaboration.
Iran shifts attacks to ships' engine rooms, inflicting damage in Persian Gulf: report
Iran's IRGC is increasingly targeting ships' engine rooms in the Persian Gulf, inflicting damage that can cripple vessels for months and trigger expensive repairs, Bloomberg reported Tuesday.
Shipping and maritime security officials reported a rise in engine-room damage, with strikes sparking fires, disabling power and propulsion systems, and leaving vessels out of service amid costly repairs.
“What we’re seeing is an increase in the frequency of attacks, and therefore, more damage in engine rooms and disabling fire,” Phillip Belcher, marine director at Intertanko, told the outlet.
“Attacks often focus on the engine room or the bridge of the ships as it maximizes damage while keeping the risk of an oil spill relatively low,” Jakob Larsen, chief safety and security officer at BIMCO, said.
He also warned that “there are significant risks of crew injuries when these areas of the ship are hit.”
Brent crude falls as investors weigh Iran talks, Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure

The November contract for U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude (CLc1), expired on Tuesday and settled $1.87 lower, or 1.8%, at $101.79 per barrel.
Iraqi PM orders indefinite closure of border crossing with Iran: report
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered the indefinite closure of the Sheeb border crossing with Iran on Tuesday, Al Jazeera reported, citing an official.
The official said the crossing would be closed to people and goods beginning Wednesday until further notice.
Several other border crossings with Iran are expected to close gradually in the coming days, the official told the outlet.
Iran says Saudi Arabia, Houthis have not responded to offer to mediate escalating conflict
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tuesday that Tehran has yet to receive a response from Saudi Arabia or Yemen's Houthi rebels regarding its offer to mediate, Reuters reported.

Iran had offered to mediate after the Houthis escalated their attacks on the kingdom.
Saudi-led coalition destroys Houthi missile launcher following attack on Riyadh
The Saudi-led coalition announced Tuesday that it had targeted and destroyed the launch platform used by Houthi forces to fire a ballistic missile at Riyadh.
“We destroyed the platform that launched the ballistic missile that was fired at Riyadh today,” coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki confirmed on X.
The coalition also shared footage showing the tracking and targeting process.
Earlier in the day, coalition forces also reported intercepting and destroying an incoming Houthi drone over the Riyadh area.
Iran blames US 'warmongering' for Hormuz crisis, demands end to threats before talks
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian demanded Tuesday that the U.S. lift sanctions and end threats before negotiations can begin, blaming American "warmongering" for regional instability and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
Speaking in Tehran with visiting Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pezeshkian blamed the United States for the ongoing conflict.
“All regional problems, from escalating tensions to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, stem from US warmongering,” Pezeshkian said, according to Iran's state-run broadcaster, IRIB.
“The Americans must explain why they started the war and embroiled themselves and the world in it.”
He added: “Before any negotiations, they must first end the pressure and threats and lift sanctions,” the president added.
Iran-linked terror probe at RAF Fairford intensifies as 2 re-arrested
British counterterrorism police re-arrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence and involvement in the suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford in September.
The arrests, made under the National Security Act, involve a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national, both from the London borough of Westminster.
"Our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement," Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said Tuesday.
He added that specialist teams are pursuing multiple lines of inquiry in what he described as a "hugely complex investigation."
The air base in Gloucestershire had been used by U.S. bombers to carry out strikes against Iran before the initial security breach when five men were arrested outside the facility.
U.S. B-1 bombers were withdrawn from the base after the arrests.

Hegseth confirms Israel visit, private Netanyahu meeting
War Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed Tuesday that he made an visited Israel on Monday and met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"I was there visiting our troops," Hegseth told reporters in Eau Claire, Wisconsin.
"Had a chance to talk to the Prime Minister. Of course, the nature of our conversations is not something I would talk about, but they've been good partners and I appreciate that."
Hegseth’s remarks follow reports that the high-level meeting took place at Ovda Air Base in southern Israel.
According to sources, the private talks centered heavily on regional security concerns, including threats posed by Iran.
Hegseth also met with U.S. service members stationed in the region under U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM).
Fox News' Liz Friden contributed to this report.
Iran blasts US arrest warrant for Cuba's Raul Castro as illegal
Tehran rejected a U.S. arrest warrant targeting former Cuban President Raul Castro on Tuesday, labeling the move an illegal and criminal act of foreign intervention.
In an official statement, the Iranian Foreign Ministry also denounced U.S. economic sanctions and intimidation tactics against Cuban officials, framing Washington's pressure campaign as a violation of the U.N. Charter and international law.
The statement followed an arrest warrant filed by Florida prosecutors charging Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.
The charges stem from his role as defense minister during the 1996 shootdown of two civilian planes operated by the exile group Brothers to the Rescue, which left four people dead.
Rubio accuses Iran of using 'Nazi U-boat tactics' to attack commercial ships in Hormuz

French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sent a joint letter in early October to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, calling on Brussels to respond more swiftly to persistent market distortions and proposing a new mechanism that could ultimately restrict foreign companies' access to the EU single market. The Franco-German document does not name its target, but it is widely seen as aimed at China.
Under the proposal, economic measures put forward by the European Commission would take effect automatically under a "reverse majority" rule—unless enough member-state governments explicitly oppose them with a qualified majority. German officials liken the design to Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, arguing that Europe likewise needs the ability to respond within days.
It marks a clear shift in Berlin's economic policy toward China. For nearly two decades, Paris has focused on reciprocal openness, industrial sovereignty and strategic dependency risks, while Berlin long believed that expanding trade and economic ties with China was broadly beneficial to the German economy. That assumption is now eroding.
The Shifting Competitive Landscape Behind a Widening Deficit
Data show Germany's exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025 while imports from China rose 8.8%, leaving a bilateral deficit of €89.3 billion (approximately $100.2 billion). In the first five months of 2026, German exports to China fell another 14.5% year on year while imports continued to climb, with auto exports hit especially hard. For the EU as a whole, goods imports from China totaled €559.4 billion (approximately $627.6 billion) in 2025 against exports of €199.6 billion (approximately $223.9 billion), a deficit of €359.8 billion (approximately $403.6 billion); compared with a decade ago, exports rose 37% and imports rose 89%.
Jeromin Zettelmeyer, director of Bruegel, summed up the shift in a single sentence during an interview on the sidelines of the Bund Summit in Shanghai on October 19: "In a sense, China is the new Germany." He argued that Chinese companies have reached the technological frontier in some fields while retaining cost advantages, meaning that even if the so-called overcapacity dispute is eased, Europe will still face structural competition from Chinese manufacturing.
In his view, European policymakers sometimes overemphasize protection without sufficiently advancing industrial restructuring. Trade policy should be judged industry by industry, rather than treating all Chinese goods as targets. Citing air conditioners as an example, he noted that as climate change drives up demand for cooling equipment in Europe, being able to import quality products at lower cost has real value.
Tariffs Can't Cure Europe's Internal Ills
Supporters of the Franco-German initiative see the trade deficit as a signal of declining competitiveness, but the scoreboard itself is easily misread. The bilateral goods deficit ignores trade in services—according to Chinese statistics, China ran a $48.3 billion services trade deficit with the EU in 2025, with the EU being the largest source of China's services trade deficit; it also ignores ownership and value added—surpluses earned by European-owned companies in China, with profits, design, patents and brand returns flowing back to Europe in large volumes. Overall, the EU still runs a goods surplus of roughly €128 billion to €133 billion (approximately $143.4 billion to $149.2 billion) with the rest of the world.
The real problems lie more within Europe itself. A European Investment Bank (EIB) survey shows that 62% of EU companies encounter difficulties when exporting to other member states, and that fragmented rules—not Chinese subsidies—are what prevent nearly two-thirds of companies from doing business within the single market. Yet Brussels is at this moment investigating whether Chinese companies distort competition.
In recent years Brussels has leaned on defensive tools. In 2024 the EU decided to impose countervailing duties on Chinese electric vehicles, on the logic of offsetting the effects of subsidies. But tariffs can only raise the prices of competitors' products; they cannot lower European companies' costs of producing batteries, shorten the cycle for developing new models, or integrate fragmented capital markets. Data show that after the EU imposed duties on Chinese EVs, sales of Chinese hybrid vehicles in Europe surged, and Brussels is now considering restrictions on hybrids—exposing the policy paradox.
Data from Rhodium Group and the Mercator Institute for China Studies show that Chinese direct investment in the EU and the UK rose 67% in 2025 to €16.8 billion (approximately $18.8 billion), with greenfield investment reaching a record €8.9 billion (approximately $10.0 billion). What tariffs mainly change is the location of production—Chinese companies are shifting toward local production, local plant construction and local hiring in Europe. The EU is thus caught in a contradiction: on one hand it wants to restrict Chinese goods, on the other it needs the jobs and supply chains that Chinese greenfield investment brings; on one hand it speaks of "de-risking," on the other Chinese companies are embedding themselves more deeply within Europe.
Who Ultimately Pays the Bill
The U.S. experience offers a reference. Papers by economists Mary Amiti, Stephen Redding and David Weinstein confirm that the tariffs imposed by the United States in 2018-2019 were almost entirely passed through to import prices, and that by the end of 2018 the U.S. had lost real income of about $1.4 billion per month—paid by American importers and consumers.
If Europe repeats the mistake, the bill will likewise fall on European companies, downstream industries and ordinary households. According to media reports, if the EU fully excluded Chinese companies and equipment in 18 sectors, EU countries would bear at least €840 billion (approximately $942.3 billion) in losses. At the same time, the EU is itself mired in energy risk: energy costs have stayed high since the Ukraine crisis, and U.S. and Israeli military strikes on Iran have further tightened global energy supplies, pushing EU natural gas prices up 50% and adding €3 billion (approximately $3.4 billion) in extra costs.
The German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK) has warned against a trade war, noting that labor costs, energy prices and bureaucratic procedures are obstacles Europe has created for itself. Spain's Público newspaper argued that it is ultimately European citizens who will pay for a trade war, suffering both higher prices and declining industrial competitiveness, and criticized EU protectionism for exposing a "double standard." Britain's The Economist, in an article titled "Europe's Industrial Woes Have Nothing to Do With Global Imbalances," argued that if Europe wants a thriving industry, it should focus on fixing its own internal problems rather than shutting competitors out.
A report published by BNP Paribas on October 5 argued that trade rebalancing cannot be achieved through trade tools alone, and that Europe should avoid repeating the U.S. government's mistake of treating the bilateral deficit as the core criterion for tariff policy. The report highlighted two keys: first, R&D spending, where the gap between Europe and China has widened markedly in recent years; second, deepening the European single market, which directly affects whether European companies can achieve the economies of scale enjoyed by China's large corporate champions.
Market Power and the Window of Time
The Franco-German initiative is not an isolated move. The Anti-Coercion Instrument adopted in 2023 is explicitly aimed at deterrence: if a third country uses economic pressure to force the EU or a member state to change policy, Brussels can respond with tariffs, services, investment and public procurement tools. When U.S. President Trump threatened to impose 30% tariffs on European goods, EU governments approved potential retaliatory tariffs on $9.3 billion of U.S. exports, with France and Germany the most active advocates of putting the Anti-Coercion Instrument on the negotiating table.
Grégoire Roos, director of the Europe, Russia and Eurasia program at Chatham House, wrote in Foreign Policy that Europe has for decades possessed a vast geopolitical asset: some 450 million relatively affluent consumers concentrated in a single regulatory space, with foreign companies eager to enter the market, so that EU rules have in effect shaped corporate behavior beyond the EU's borders—the so-called "Brussels effect."
But he also cautioned that market power is useful only as long as Europe remains indispensable to China's economy, and that balance is shifting rapidly, especially in key industries such as batteries, clean technology and electric vehicles. Trade defense alone will not bring cheaper energy or create technological leadership. Protecting an industry and making it competitive are two different things. The Franco-German document is a positive signal, but the bigger challenge is that Paris and Berlin still need to push reforms to revive flagging competitiveness; once the so-called unfair competition issue is resolved, the real hard battle—domestic economic reform—will only just be beginning.
The European Union Chamber of Commerce in China's 2026 survey shows that 94% of member companies consider China an important sourcing location, and 48% believe Chinese companies are more innovative than European competitors. A DIHK survey in early September showed that 83% of respondents felt intensifying competition from Chinese companies, yet 88% still wanted to continue the businesses affected; in response, 60% chose to rely on innovation, 50% on cost reduction and 39% on opening new markets.

The Pound to US Dollar (GBP/USD) exchange rate moved higher on Tuesday after unexpectedly strong UK employment figures reinforced expectations that the Bank of England (BoE) will raise interest rates in November.
At the time of writing, GBP/USD was trading at around $1.3346, up approximately 0.3% from Tuesday's opening levels.
Sterling found fresh support after the latest UK labour market report delivered a considerably stronger performance than economists had anticipated.
Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed the unemployment rate fell from 4.9% to 4.7% in the three months to August, defying expectations for a broadly unchanged reading.
Employment also increased by 102,000, comfortably exceeding forecasts for a rise of just 20,000.
Wage growth provided further encouragement for Pound investors.
Regular earnings, excluding bonuses, accelerated from 3.6% to 3.7% year-on-year, suggesting that underlying pay pressures remain persistent despite earlier signs of a cooling labour market.

The US Dollar (USD), meanwhile, struggled to attract demand on Tuesday as improving market sentiment reduced appetite for traditional safe-haven currencies.
Although oil prices remained elevated and concerns persisted over the possibility of renewed escalation in the Middle East, investors showed a greater willingness to hold riskier assets.
Expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates more gradually than previously anticipated also limited support for the 'Greenback'.
US political developments added another source of uncertainty.
Recent polling suggesting stronger support for the Democrats ahead of the mid-term elections raised questions over whether President Donald Trump could face greater opposition to his legislative agenda.

Near-Term GBP/USD Forecast: UK Inflation Could Extend Sterling's Gains
Wednesday's UK consumer price index (CPI) release will provide the next major test for the Pound to US Dollar exchange rate.

Following Tuesday's stronger employment figures, an above-forecast inflation reading would strengthen the case for another Bank of England rate increase in November.
This could allow Sterling to build on its latest gains and challenge the $1.3400 level.
However, a softer inflation reading could temper expectations for further tightening and encourage some profit-taking following the Pound's recent recovery.
For the US Dollar, the absence of major economic releases may leave broader market sentiment as the main influence on trading.
Renewed geopolitical tensions or a deterioration in risk appetite could revive demand for the safe-haven Dollar, potentially limiting GBP/USD's upside.

Key Investor Takeaways
- Copper One Resources Corp. has agreed to acquire a 100% interest in the Sword & Gossan nickel-copper-cobalt properties in Labrador for CA$3.65 million in purchase consideration, plus CA$400,000 in scheduled advance royalty payments, bringing total scheduled cash commitments to CA$4.05 million and expanding its North American critical metals exploration portfolio.
- The 3,900-hectare Sword & Gossan property includes 156 mineral claims covering a historically explored nickel-copper-cobalt sulphide system, with multiple untested electromagnetic conductors, surface mineralization, and historical drill intercepts.
- Copper One's flagship Majuba Hill copper project in Nevada has undergone more than 90,000 feet of drilling across more than 100 holes. The company expanded its planned 2026 Phase 2 diamond drilling program to up to 10,000 feet to test priority targets and advance the project toward a maiden mineral resource estimate.
- AI-assisted copper exploration at Majuba Hill uses ExploreTech geological modeling to identify drilling targets. The company's 2025 drilling included an AI-designed hole that intersected copper mineralization associated with the South Resistivity Anomaly.
- Copper One's 2026 exploration milestones include advancing Phase 2 drilling at Majuba Hill, evaluating priority breccia targets, refining its three-dimensional geological model, and continuing work toward a maiden NI 43-101-compliant mineral resource estimate.
Copper One Expands Critical Minerals Portfolio With CA$3.65 Million Labrador Acquisition
Copper One Resources Corp. (CEXY:CSE; CEXYF:OTCPK; IW8:FSE) announced that it had entered into a purchase and sale agreement to acquire a 100% interest in the Sword & Gossan Mineral Properties in west-central Labrador, Newfoundland and Labrador.
The agreement, dated October 6, 2026, was entered into with 1594122 B.C. Ltd., an arm's-length vendor. The acquisition covers ten mineral licenses comprising 156 claims across approximately 3,900 hectares, located about 90 kilometers north of Churchill Falls on the northern side of the Smallwood Reservoir.
The property includes the historical Sword, also known as Michikamau, nickel-copper-cobalt project, where previous operators conducted airborne geophysical surveys, geological mapping, surface sampling, and initial drilling. That work identified a magmatic sulphide system containing nickel-copper-cobalt mineralization, along with multiple electromagnetic conductors that have not been drill-tested.
The central unanswered question is whether the electromagnetic conductors identified at Sword & Gossan represent substantial nickel-copper-cobalt sulphide mineralization. Although historical reports described mineralized showings and drilling that intersected sulphides at the Juno conductive zone, most of the property's electromagnetic targets remain untested by drilling. Additional exploration, laboratory analysis, and geological evaluation will be required to determine whether these targets contain mineralization of sufficient grade, size, and continuity to warrant further development studies.
"The proposed acquisition of Sword & Gossan would expand Copper One's North American critical metals portfolio with a nickel-copper-cobalt exploration opportunity in Labrador," said David Greenway, President and CEO of Copper One, in the company's news release. "Historical surface sampling and drilling identified mineralization, while multiple electromagnetic conductors remain untested."
Under the agreement, Copper One will pay the vendor CA$3.65 million in cash, consisting of an initial CA$1.15 million payment due one business day after the agreement's effective date and a second payment of CA$2.5 million within six months of execution. In addition, the company is required to make two advance royalty payments of CA$200,000 each on the first and second anniversaries of the effective date, bringing total scheduled cash commitments to CA$4.05 million, excluding any optional royalty buyback. No company securities will be issued as part of the acquisition.
The property is subject to an existing 2% net smelter returns royalty payable to its underlying owner. Copper One has the option to purchase 1% of that royalty for CA$2 million in cash at any time through written notice, reducing the aggregate royalty to 1%.
Completion of the transaction remains subject to due diligence, board approvals, required third-party consents, Canadian Securities Exchange acceptance, and the absence of a material adverse change in the property's status before closing. No finder's fees are payable.
The Sword project area consists of seven licenses covering 57 claims and 1,425 hectares, while Gossan comprises three licenses covering 99 claims and 2,475 hectares. The vendor has represented that the licenses are in good standing, with CA$31,200 in assessment expenditures due between July and August 2027.
The property lies within the Michikamau Intrusion, one of Labrador's largest anorthosite-troctolite intrusive complexes, and approximately 300 kilometers southwest of the Voisey's Bay nickel-copper-cobalt mine.
Historical exploration conducted between 2005 and 2007 identified multiple electromagnetic conductors that geophysical consultants interpreted as potentially consistent in intensity and geometry with massive sulphide bodies. Most remain untested by drilling. Copper One cautioned in its October 7, 2026, announcement that a qualified person had not completed sufficient work to verify the historical exploration results and that the company was not treating them as current. The historical interpretations and electromagnetic anomalies do not establish the presence, grade, continuity, or economic viability of mineralization.
Historical surface prospecting reported nickel, copper, and cobalt mineralization at several gossanous showings, including Gossan 115 and Sword Far North. At the Juno conductive zone, a historical two-hole drilling program reportedly intersected nickel-copper-cobalt sulphide mineralization across a broad interval. The previous operator's assessment report recommended deeper drilling to investigate a possible feeder system.
The conductors occur within troctolite and leuco-troctolite host rocks, which previous geological interpretations associated with a possible feeder zone to the Michikamau Intrusion.
Copper, Nickel, and Cobalt Markets Reflect Shifting Supply and Demand
According to Trading Economics on October 13, copper traded at US$6.7148 per pound, up 0.24% for the day, 6.08% over the previous month, and 35.05% year over year. The publication reported that copper futures had climbed toward US$6.70 per pound, approaching record highs amid supply disruptions in Chile, the world's largest copper producer.
On the demand side, increased orders associated with data centers, semiconductor development, artificial intelligence infrastructure, battery storage, and electric vehicles across Asia continued to support the market outlook. Falling oil prices also provided support by potentially easing inflationary pressures and reducing expectations for aggressive U.S. Federal Reserve monetary tightening.
Trading Economics on October 8 described cobalt as a "hard, lustrous, gray metal with a high melting point (1493°C)." Its reported applications included chemicals, superalloys for gas turbine blades and aircraft engines, specialized steel, carbides, diamond tools, and magnets. Chemical production accounted for approximately 58% of cobalt use, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo represented more than half of global production.
In its nickel market commentary, Trading Economics reported that "Nickel fell to around US$15,600 per tonne, hitting its lowest level since December 2025 as ample availability continued to weigh on prices."
The report identified increased Philippine nickel ore shipments to Indonesia and rising London Metal Exchange inventories as factors contributing to available supply. Exchange inventories had climbed to 278,898 tonnes by September 24 from an August low of 264,444 tonnes.
Nickel consumption remained concentrated in stainless steel production, while battery demand provided a more limited contribution. The report also described production constraints in Indonesia, including ore quota restrictions and water shortages that had affected some smelting operations.
Together, the October market data showed differing conditions across the three metals, with copper recording substantial annual price gains, nickel posting a smaller yearly increase despite recent weakness, and cobalt experiencing declines over both monthly and annual periods.
Exploration Programs and Resource Definition Plans at Majuba Hill
Separate from the proposed Labrador acquisition, Copper One outlined drilling activities, exploration targets, and resource-definition objectives at its flagship Majuba Hill copper-silver-gold project in Pershing County, Nevada.
Majuba Hill covers approximately 9,684 acres, or 3,919 hectares, comprising 403 federal lode mining claims and two private parcels. The property is located approximately 70 miles southwest of Winnemucca and 156 miles northeast of Reno, with a power substation approximately 22 miles from the site.
Copper One reported more than 90,000 feet, or 27,127 meters, of drilling across more than 110 holes at Majuba Hill. The company completed multiple drilling phases between 2020 and 2025, including five diamond drill holes totaling 5,484.5 feet, or 1,671.7 meters, during 2025.
The 2025 program included drill hole MHB-32, which intersected a 115.7-meter interval grading 0.33% copper and 16.97 parts per million silver. high_priority_articles.title: Kallas: Russian Black Sea strikes deepen ‘perfect storm’ for world food supplies - Euronews
high_priority_articles.summary: Kallas: Russian Black Sea strikes deepen ‘perfect storm’ for world food supplies  EuronewsNato increases Black Sea deployment amid escalating deadly Russian attacks  The GuardianNATO to send planes and drones to Black Sea after attacks on shipping  ReutersSeven crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast  BBCRussia trying to limit Ukrainian export routes - Kallas  RTE.ie
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Ukraine is losing an estimated €60 million a day in export earnings as Moscow is accused of targetting the routes it uses to ship grain abroad.
Suspected Russian drone strikes on civilian shipping in the Black Sea are piling further pressure on global food supplies, the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has warned.
Addressing the European Parliament on Tuesday, Kallas said vessels had come under attack six times in 10 days, describing it as "a dangerous and unacceptable escalation".
The strikes have hit ships off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, both EU and NATO members, prompting alarm across Europe.
Kallas, the High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, accused the Kremlin of trying to choke off Ukraine’s income while Russian troops make little progress on the battlefield. She said Ukraine was losing around €60 million a day in export revenue.
Ukraine is one of the world’s leading exporters of wheat, maize and barley, most of which leaves the country by sea.
Kallas said global grain reserves were in better shape than in 2022, when a Russian blockade left 20 million tonnes of Ukrainian grain stranded.
"Global grain stockpiles are larger than in 2022," she said. "But the global food system is now facing a perfect storm: a super El Nino, drought in both hemispheres, and conflict in the Middle East, straining fertiliser exports."
But she warned of a combination of threats: a super El Niño, drought in both hemispheres, and conflict in the Middle East disrupting fertiliser exports.
"Russia’s actions make it harder to put food on people’s plates across the world," she said.
Back-up routes at risk
Since 2022, the EU has built overland "solidarity lanes" to carry Ukrainian goods through its member states instead of across the Black Sea. Kallas said these were now under threat too, as Russia targets border crossings with Moldova, Romania and Poland.
Last week, EU leaders called for safe passage for civilian shipping in the Black Sea to be restored immediately.
NATO to deploy 'additional assets'
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart announced later on Tuesday that the alliance would be sending "additional assets" to the Black Sea region following the recent wave of drone incidents.
"NATO will be sending additional assets to the region, including support for surveillance, reconnaissance, and forensics," Hart wrote in a post on social media.
"We will continue to stand united and ensure that we are ready and able to address any threat and to keep our one billion people safe."

high_priority_articles.title: ‘Deal pretty close’: Trump on India-US trade agreement - The Siasat Daily
high_priority_articles.summary: ‘Deal pretty close’: Trump on India-US trade agreement  The Siasat Daily
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump said that India wants to conclude a trade agreement with the United States and indicated that the two countries were close to reaching a deal, while suggesting that the final arrangement would differ significantly from earlier trade agreements.
Speaking to reporters during an Oval Office interaction alongside Vice President JD Vance, Trump responded to a question about whether Washington and New Delhi were approaching an agreement.
“They want to make a deal. We’re going to make a deal pretty close,” Trump said.
“Yeah, that’s going to be a much different kind of deal than we’ve made,” he added.
The remarks came as Secretary of State Marco Rubio was visiting India and holding discussions with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, placing the President’s comments against the backdrop of high-level diplomatic engagement between the two countries.
Trump did not elaborate on what would make the proposed agreement different from previous arrangements.
He also did not specify a date for concluding negotiations or identify the remaining issues preventing a final agreement.
The President’s comments nevertheless suggested that Washington expected progress in talks that have been closely watched by businesses, exporters and investors in both countries.
India and the United States have been negotiating a bilateral trade arrangement aimed at expanding market access and addressing longstanding differences over tariffs, agricultural products, industrial goods and regulatory barriers.
Trade negotiations have acquired additional significance under Trump’s second administration, which has made tariffs and reciprocal market access central elements of American economic policy.
The administration has argued that trading partners must offer American businesses greater access to their markets while reducing barriers affecting US exports.
For India, the negotiations carry implications for major export sectors, including pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, textiles, electronics and information technology-related services.
American companies have also sought greater opportunities in India’s expanding consumer market and manufacturing sectors.
The President’s latest remarks did not indicate whether negotiators had resolved differences over specific sectors or reached agreement on tariff reductions.
Nor did he announce any new investment commitments, market-access concessions or implementation timetable.
The comments came during an Oval Office event primarily devoted to the administration’s efforts to combat fraud involving federal government programmes.
Trump and Vance announced new incentives for individuals reporting suspected misuse of taxpayer funds and discussed the administration’s broader economic priorities.
During the interaction, Trump also spoke about reducing American trade deficits with major trading partners.
He cited Canada, Mexico and the European Union while arguing that his administration’s trade policies were changing longstanding commercial relationships.
The President said the United States was experiencing strong economic growth and attracting substantial new investment in manufacturing and industrial facilities.
He presented the administration’s tariff and trade strategy as part of a wider effort to strengthen domestic production and employment.
Although Trump did not discuss India’s tariffs or trade surplus during the exchange, his remarks about the proposed agreement came within that broader economic context.
The President’s comments followed months of discussions between officials in Washington and New Delhi over the terms of a bilateral trade arrangement.
Both governments have identified trade and investment as important pillars of the relationship, alongside defence cooperation, technology partnerships and energy security.
The United States is among India’s largest trading partners, with bilateral commerce spanning goods and services. The economic relationship also includes substantial investment flows and commercial partnerships involving technology, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing and financial services.

high_priority_articles.title: ‘Tariffs Are Not Meant To Punish India’: Marco Rubio Says US-India Trade Deal Is Close - Outlook India
high_priority_articles.summary: ‘Tariffs Are Not Meant To Punish India’: Marco Rubio Says US-India Trade Deal Is Close  Outlook India
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- Marco Rubio says US tariffs on India are part of Washington’s broader foreign policy response to Russia’s war against Ukraine, not an attempt to punish New Delhi.
- The US secretary of state says the India-US trade agreement is close to completion, although some issues remain unresolved.
- Russian oil imports, immigration restrictions and visa policies remain points of friction as the two countries seek to strengthen their strategic and economic partnership.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said American tariffs on India were not intended to “punish or harm” the country, arguing that the measures form part of Washington’s wider foreign policy response to Russia’s war against Ukraine. Speaking during his visit to India, Rubio said the United States wanted the conflict to end, as New Delhi and Washington work to finalise a long-delayed trade agreement amid tensions over tariffs and India’s purchases of Russian oil.
“None of these tariffs are done to punish or harm India,” Rubio said in an interview with The Indian Express, adding that they were part of a broader foreign policy approach shaped by the war in Ukraine. His remarks appeared aimed at addressing Indian concerns over US trade measures, which have complicated efforts to strengthen economic ties between the two countries.
Trade Deal Nears Completion Amid Tariff Dispute
Rubio said the India-US trade agreement was “incredibly close” to completion, with most of the work finished and only a small number of issues remaining. The negotiations have been underway for more than a year and a half, but progress has been held up by disagreements over tariffs, market access and India’s continued purchases of Russian crude. Rubio’s comments suggest both sides are seeking to move past the dispute, although no final agreement has been announced.
During his Mumbai visit, Rubio held talks with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on trade, energy, defence, technology and regional developments. The two sides also discussed strengthening the wider strategic partnership. The talks came days after US President Donald Trump waived potential additional tariffs linked to India’s Russian oil purchases, easing one immediate source of pressure on bilateral trade negotiations.
Russian Oil And Visa Restrictions Remain Points Of Friction
India’s purchases of Russian crude have been a major source of tension with Washington since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The US has pressed countries to reduce their reliance on Russian energy as part of efforts to limit Moscow’s revenue, while India has defended its energy decisions on the grounds of national interest and supply security. Rubio’s comments acknowledge the geopolitical context of the tariffs but do not remove the wider differences between the two countries over energy and trade.
Rubio also defended the Trump administration’s immigration restrictions, saying they were intended to address longstanding weaknesses in the US immigration system rather than target India specifically. His comments come amid Indian concerns over visa policies and their impact on skilled workers and technology companies. The trade negotiations, energy cooperation and immigration rules remain important tests for a relationship both governments describe as strategically significant.
As Rubio continues his India visit, the immediate challenge for both governments is to translate the improved tone into progress on outstanding economic issues. His assurance that the tariffs were not intended as punishment signals an effort to ease tensions, but the durability of the reset will depend on whether the two sides can conclude the trade agreement and manage their differences over Russia, energy and immigration.

high_priority_articles.title: Marco Rubio In India: Can US Biz Diplomacy Ease Trump Tensions Over Tariffs, Russian Oil And Bring Trade Deal Closer? - Menafn
high_priority_articles.summary: Marco Rubio In India: Can US Biz Diplomacy Ease Trump Tensions Over Tariffs, Russian Oil And Bring Trade Deal Closer?  Menafn
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Rubio, who arrived in Mumbai on October 20 for a three-day visit, described India as a global“refining superpower” and said Washington would discuss opportunities for Reliance to process more Venezuelan crude at its Indian refineries.
He also indicated that the Indian conglomerate could explore producing oil in Venezuela.
The visit comes at a sensitive juncture in India-US relations, with trade disputes and tariff tensions persisting even as New Delhi continues to buy Russian crude to diversify its energy supplies and safeguard its energy security.
However, US President Donald Trump 's recent decision to waive potential sanctions-related tariffs on major buyers of Russian crude could remove one significant obstacle to a bilateral trade agreement, as per Reuters report.
Against this backdrop, Rubio's engagements with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai and Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani in Jamnagar underscore the importance Washington is placing on commercial and energy diplomacy alongside its broader strategic partnership with India.
India-US trade deal: 'Very, very close', says Rubio
Rubio struck an optimistic note on the long-pending India-US trade agreement, saying the negotiations were nearing completion, with only a few issues left to resolve.
“We're very, very close. I would say we're about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement,” Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday.
Following the meeting between Jaishankar and Rubio, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA ) said the two sides discussed a broad range of issues, including trade, defence, technology and energy security.
“They welcomed the progress made in negotiations on the India–U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA ) and reaffirmed their commitment to working towards its early conclusion,” the MEA said in a statement.
The ministers also exchanged views on regional and global developments, according to the ministry.
Why is Rubio visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar instead of Delhi?
One of the most striking aspects of Rubio's itinerary is its emphasis on India's and industrial centres rather than New Delhi, where high-level diplomatic engagements with visiting US officials would ordinarily be expected to take place.
Mumbai provides access to corporate leaders and financial institutions, while Jamnagar in Gujarat is home to Reliance Industries' twin refineries, which together form the world's largest single-location refining complex.
Also Read | India-US trade deal 'very close' to completion, Marco Rubio says
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor has said that the visit would have a stronger focus, with Rubio scheduled to meet government officials in Mumbai and business representatives in Jamnagar.
Suresh K Goel, a former Indian diplomat, said the choice of locations raised questions about the nature of the visit and the agenda behind the engagements.
“If the Ministry of External Affairs prepared the programme, I do find it that this meeting was not scheduled earlier in Delhi and that he was going to Mumbai or to Jamnagar. Clearly, the agenda for the meeting was not official talks or anything,” Goel told LiveMint.
Why is Reliance Industries important to the US energy agenda?
Rubio's planned engagement with Reliance highlights the role India's refining capacity could play in Washington's efforts to expand markets for Venezuelan crude.
The US secretary of state said Washington would discuss encouraging Reliance to refine more Venezuelan oil at its Indian facilities and potentially explore oil production opportunities in Venezuela.
Reliance operates a massive refining complex in Jamnagar, giving it the capacity to process a wide range of crude grades. Its role could therefore be significant in any effort to expand the flow of Venezuelan oil to India.
For Washington, the discussions offer a potential commercial avenue for strengthening energy ties with India.
Rubio's visit is also expected to include a meeting with Reliance chairman Mukesh Ambani, bringing one of India's largest corporate groups into discussions that extend beyond conventional government-to-government diplomacy.
Russian oil, Trump's tariff threat and the road to a trade deal
Trump's administration had authorised the possibility of imposing tariffs of up to 100% on major importers of Russian oil, a measure that could have affected India, the world's second-largest buyer of Russian crude after China.
However, Trump recently waived potential tariffs targeting major buyers of Russian oil, removing one possible stumbling block in the trade negotiations with New Delhi, as per a Reuters report.
The move has also drawn criticism from US lawmakers who argue that Washington has been insufficiently tough on Moscow.
Why the strategic partnership still matters
Despite the strains over trade and Russian oil, India remains an important partner for the United States because of its economic potential, democratic institutions and cooperation across multiple strategic sectors, according to Goel.
Goel cautioned against allowing trade disputes or differences in diplomatic approach to overshadow the broader relationship.
“The relationship between India and the USA is very, very important in all respects. And therefore, the government, rather than becoming part of this temperament or trade effect kind of a thing, has to be mature in our dealing and try and see how we can actually conduct the relationship,” Goel told LiveMint.
He also emphasised India's significance as a democratic and economic partner for Washington in Asia.
“India continues to be important for the USA as an economic and democratic partner. After all, if you look at Asia, which is the other democracy which can compare in terms of relationship?” Goel said.

high_priority_articles.title: The decline of South Africa's mining sector: Challenges and opportunities - weekendargus.co.za
high_priority_articles.summary: The decline of South Africa's mining sector: Challenges and opportunities  weekendargus.co.za
high_priority_articles.full_text:
A new Bureau for Economic Research (BER) document indicated that South Africa’s mining sector has been in decline in recent years but still has potential to be a force globally.
Robert Botha from BER said that the economic history of South Africa is intimately bound to the extraction of its mineral wealth.
“Despite this geological lottery, the sector faces various constraints that have prevented it from taking full advantage of successive commodity booms. Once the primary engine of the economy, the sector’s economic contribution has stagnated, allowing the notion to take hold that South African mining is a sunset sector,” Botha said.
Botha added that despite successive commodity price booms, in real terms the sector has declined since 1994. “Over this period, the sector contracted by 0.29% on average. By 2024, the sector was nearly 12% smaller than it was in 1994. The long-term performance of the South African mining sector is defined by a significant structural decline that began in the 1970s. A collapsing gold sector, once the backbone of the economy, reduced aggregate mining production volumes.”
Botha said the most profound evidence of structural failure occurred during the global "Missed Super-Cycle" (2001–2008). “While peer resource-rich nations like Australia saw mining investment and GDP surge due to Chinese industrialisation, South Africa’s mining contribution actually shrank by 1%. Research indicates that this divergence was largely driven by domestic policy transitions rather than geology.”
Botha added that the trajectory of investor confidence, as tracked by the Fraser Institute, reveals a steady descent. “South Africa transitioned from a premier investment destination in the early 2000s to a bottom-tier jurisdiction by 2024. This decline was accelerated by the policy shock era (2004–2010), followed by a crisis of confidence era (2011–2017) which was marked by labour unrest and state-led corruption.”
Botha said despite a long-term decline in real terms, the South African mining sector remains a cornerstone of the national economy. “In 2024, the industry directly contributed R442 billion, representing 6% of the nominal GDP. Beyond its direct output, the sector functions as a vital economic engine through significant multiplier effects. The Minerals Council estimates an employment multiplier of ten, meaning every direct mining job supports ten additional opportunities in other sectors.”
Botha added that the sector is the primary anchor for South Africa’s external trade balance, accounting for over 50% of all merchandise export earnings. “This trade surplus provides a critical cushion for the current account, helping to offset structural deficits caused by the importation of machinery and refined fuels.”
Botha said that between 2018 and 2024, the sector accounted for between 6.5% and 10.9% of total national revenue through corporate income tax, mining royalties, and personal income tax. “In real terms, the industry has shrunk by 11.5% since 1994, exerting a persistent drag on national GDP growth. This decline is primarily driven by the collapse of the gold sector, which saw an 84% reduction in output over this period. However, if gold production is excluded, the rest of the sector actually grew by 41%, revealing a stark divergence in sub-sector performance.”
Botha added that mining employment has steadily contracted from its 1987 peak of over 760,000 jobs to approximately 465,000 today, reflecting a disconnect between rising wages and stagnating labour productivity. “Furthermore, the sector faces a capital productivity paradox where increased fixed capital formation, which reached R159 billion in 2024, fails to translate into higher volumes due to external constraints.”
Botha said South Africa possesses one of the world's most significant mineral endowments. “The country holds the world’s largest reserves of Platinum Group Metals (PGMs) and manganese, as well as the second largest deposits of chromium, positioning it as an indispensable anchor in global industrial value chains. Despite this wealth, the sector's full potential remains largely latent: with only 9% to 14% of the country geo-mapped at a detailed 1:50,000 scale, significant discoveries likely remain untapped.”
Botha added that structurally, the industry is split between large-cap multinational majors and a vital but struggling junior mining sector. “The majors—such as Anglo American and Glencore—operate at a massive scale, focusing on brownfields exploration to extend the life of existing assets. Junior miners serve as the industry’s research-and-development arm, focusing on high-risk greenfields exploration. The long-term health of the industry depends on a functional relationship where juniors discover new deposits and majors bring them into production.”

high_priority_articles.title: Initiatives of Uzbekistan aimed at Economic Results for the Countries of Central Asia and Azerbaijan - DKNews.kz
high_priority_articles.summary: Initiatives of Uzbekistan aimed at Economic Results for the Countries of Central Asia and Azerbaijan  DKNews.kz
high_priority_articles.full_text:
On October 8–9, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev attended the 8th Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, as well as a meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State.
The consultative meetings stem from an initiative put forward by the President of Uzbekistan in 2017. The first meeting took place in Astana in March 2018. This framework allows countries to work together on transit, infrastructure use, border procedures and industrial cooperation where the involvement of several countries is required.
At the seventh meeting, held in Tashkent on November 16, 2025, participants agreed to Azerbaijan’s full participation. This creates opportunities to coordinate industrial development in Central Asia with transport infrastructure in the South Caucasus and routes to markets in Türkiye and Europe.
For businesses, transport arrangements need to be coordinated along the entire route. Faster customs clearance in one country will have limited benefits if cargo is held up at the next border or port. Joint ventures also need coordinated arrangements for raw material supplies, certification and financing. Expanding the group of participants therefore makes multilateral coordination more useful in practice.
Expanding Trade and the Regional Market
According to the Center for Economic Research and Reforms (CERR), Uzbekistan’s trade with Central Asian countries grew 3.1-fold between 2017 and 2025, reaching $8.3 billion. In 2025, trade with Kazakhstan totaled $5 billion, with Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan $1.2 billion each, and with Tajikistan $912.3 million.
In January–August 2026, trade with the four neighboring countries reached $6.14 billion, up 26.2% from the same period a year earlier. Uzbekistan’s exports rose 37.5% to $2.36 billion, while imports increased 20.1% to $3.78 billion. Trade grew with every partner: Kazakhstan by 23.4%, Kyrgyzstan by 51.2%, Tajikistan by 45.7% and Turkmenistan by 5.7%.
Trade with Azerbaijan grew 9.5-fold between 2017 and 2025, reaching $307.3 million. In 2025, Uzbekistan’s exports totaled $227.3 million and imports $80 million. Established trade in machinery, textiles, food and metals provides a basis for greater specialization among businesses and joint efforts to promote their products. Long-term contracts, well-developed distribution networks and equipment servicing in the partner country can support more sustained growth.
Investment and Production Links
Between 2017 and 2025, Uzbekistan attracted $2.5 billion in foreign direct investment and loans from Central Asian countries, including $1.3 billion in 2025. The corresponding figures for Azerbaijan were $318.6 million and $173.7 million. As of August 2026, Uzbekistan had 2,538 operating companies with investment from Central Asian countries and 503 with Azerbaijani investment.
The Azerbaijan–Uzbekistan Investment Company supports joint projects and has charter capital of $500 million. Joint investment institutions also operate in Central Asia, including Uzbek–Kyrgyz and Uzbek–Tajik institutions. They enable partners to finance projects together and share risks.
Practical Steps Since the Tashkent Meeting
On November 17, 2025, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan launched the Shavat–Dashoguz border trade zone. It houses trading and warehousing facilities, customs, quarantine and other inspection services. Government services are to be provided through a single-window system.
On March 26, 2026, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan launched ten joint projects in furniture, leather and textile production, household appliances and other industries. At the same time, facilities were launched to produce dairy products in Andijan Region, and fruit juices and metal briquettes in Surkhandarya Region.
During Uzbek–Kyrgyz talks on July 30, 2026, the two sides agreed to establish an Interstate Council. A package of trade contracts and investment agreements was put together at the preceding business forum. They also reached agreements on developing border, trade and logistics infrastructure along the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway and digitizing permit procedures.
On July 31, 2026, the leaders of Central Asia and Azerbaijan held an informal meeting at Issyk-Kul. The President of Uzbekistan called for further work on industrial and technological production chains, shared digital services and investment platforms.
On August 23, 2026, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan signed a program to increase trade to $1 billion by 2030, along with an action plan for investment and trade. The third meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council also launched joint projects in finance, building materials, oil and gas, mining, agriculture and other sectors.
Industrial Cooperation and Access to New Markets
CERR estimates that replacing some imports from third countries with supplies from within the region could increase intraregional trade by approximately $11.4 billion. Realizing this potential will depend on whether regional suppliers can compete. This requires matching imported products with what regional producers can offer and identifying barriers to concluding contracts.
Developing the Middle Corridor through the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus could expand Uzbekistan’s opportunities to supply markets to the west. The route’s competitiveness depends on the total cost of delivery, regular departures and transit times along each section. This requires coordination among railways, ports, carriers and customs services.
Joint preparations for the Kambarata-1 hydropower plant and work on Uzbek–Tajik hydropower projects require agreement on financing, water use arrangements and electricity supply terms. Investment decisions need to reflect growing industrial demand and businesses’ need for reliable energy supplies.
An interagency working group has also been established to prepare joint green energy projects involving Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan.
Priorities for the Upcoming Meeting
The upcoming meeting in Avaza offers an opportunity to advance joint projects by addressing trade barriers, coordinating transport arrangements and securing financing. Moving beyond separate bilateral projects to align business conditions across the expanded group of participating countries could help advance these efforts.
Projects backed by proven demand, competitive production and reliable logistics can deliver the most tangible economic benefits. The regional mechanisms proposed by Uzbekistan could support these projects by removing trade barriers, coordinating infrastructure development and improving investment conditions. Under these conditions, growth in trade within the region would be accompanied by more value added within the region and a stronger position for its producers in international markets.
Edvard Romanov
Center for Economic Research and Reforms

South Korea's exports surged in October, driven by strong AI chip demand and highlighting economic resilience ahead of the central bank's interest-rate decision. Semiconductor shipments led the gains, jumping over 220 percent year on year.
South Korea's exports continued to grow at a rapid pace in the first 20 days of October, driven by strong global demand for artificial intelligence (AI), which boosted chip shipments and highlighted the economy's resilience a day before the central bank's interest-rate decision.
Exports adjusted for the number of working days rose 65.9% year on year, the country's customs office said on Wednesday, October 21. This was slower than the 89.8% increase recorded over the same period in September.

Without the adjustment, exports climbed 105.4% to $61.6 billion, while imports rose 42.8%, leaving the country with a trade surplus of $14.5 billion. Exports had totalled $71.4 billion in the first 20 days of September.
However, the unadjusted year-on-year figures were difficult to compare because the Chuseok holidays fell in September this year, but in October last year. The working-day-adjusted figure therefore provided a more reliable indication of the underlying trend.
Semiconductors led the gains, with chip exports surging 222.5% to $27.5 billion. Shipments of petroleum products rose 68.3%, while car exports increased by almost 41%.
By destination, shipments to China jumped 154.4%, while exports to the United States rose 154.9%. Exports to Malaysia climbed 363.2%, while those to Singapore increased 121.1%.
The figures provided the Bank of Korea (BOK) with an additional economic indicator ahead of Thursday's policy decision. The central bank was widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged as it assessed the impact of its recent rate rises.
The Bank of Korea (BOK) raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3% earlier in August, marking its second consecutive increase. The move came after stronger-than-expected economic growth and persistent inflation prompted policymakers to act early.

On October 21, stock markets in Japan and South Korea strengthened in tandem, with memory chip stocks serving as the main force driving the indices higher. The Nikkei 225 opened at 64,885.95, up 1.26%, while South Korea's KOSPI opened up 2% at 5,666.34. Gains widened further after the open, with the Nikkei 225 rising as much as 2%, a gain of nearly 1,300 points, while the KOSPI extended its advance to 3.37%.
At the individual stock level, South Korea's two major memory chipmakers stood out. Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) rose more than 4% intraday, while SK Hynix (000660.KS) gained more than 6%. Shares of South Korean data center technology company Elice jumped 16%, after the stock had plunged 32% on its first day of trading in South Korea.
The rebound came after the KOSPI suffered a sharp decline the previous day. On October 20, the index turned lower after two straight sessions of modest gains, closing down 215.27 points, or 3.73%, its lowest close since April 7. It fell as much as 4.76% intraday, losing the 5,500-point mark. On the flows side, foreign investors and domestic institutions sold in tandem that day: foreign investors recorded net sales of ₩636.7 billion (approximately $480.2 million) on South Korea's securities market, while institutional investors sold a net ₩467 billion (approximately $352.2 million), of which financial investment institutions sold a net ₩241.8 billion (approximately $182.4 million) and pension funds sold a net ₩159 billion (approximately $119.9 million). Individual investors and other corporate entities bought a net ₩838.8 billion (approximately $632.7 million) and ₩261.6 billion (approximately $197.3 million), respectively.
