On the macroeconomic front, Japan's September imports rose 18.9% year-on-year, versus an estimate of 20.4%, while exports rose 16.7%, versus an estimate of 21.3%, with both readings below market expectations. South Korea's September producer price index (PPI) rose 7.7% year-on-year.
Overnight, the three major U.S. stock indices closed mixed, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down 0.29%, as 11 constituents advanced and 19 declined. Lam Research fell 3.21%, ARM dropped 3.07%, ASML slipped 0.99%, AMD lost 0.62%, Intel declined 0.37% and Broadcom edged down 0.07%. Memory-related stocks were similarly mixed: Western Digital rose 3.44%, Seagate Technology gained 2.17%, SanDisk fell 0.42%, Micron Technology dropped 0.98% and SK Hynix declined 2.16%.
On the recent weakness in South Korean stocks, JPMorgan offered its assessment in a latest report. The bank argued that South Korean equities are quite cheap by both share price levels and trading metrics, but buyers willing to keep adding positions are disappearing. The report cited a marked slowdown in share buybacks by listed companies as an important reason for the recent decline: buybacks had been the main force supporting the market since late August, but Samsung Electronics has completed its buyback program and SK Hynix's is nearing completion.
Valuation data support that assessment. According to the report, even excluding the two memory chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the KOSPI's forward price-to-earnings ratio is just 8.4 times, a level lower than it has been about 90% of the time by historical standards. Meanwhile, market expectations for the future earnings of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix were repeatedly raised in October, with upgrades particularly pronounced in the industrials, financials and health care sectors. That implies the selloff was driven more by capital flight and risk aversion than by a broad deterioration in corporate profitability.
Still, short-term liquidity conditions remain fragile. JPMorgan estimates that quantitative funds such as CTAs, which automatically buy and sell based on price trends, likely shifted from heavily bullish to betting on declines after the latest rout; with short positions already sizable and share prices clearly oversold, conditions for a short-term rebound are forming. But the bank also cautioned that leveraged funds tracking South Korean stocks remain large in scale and outflows have been limited, and such funds often need to sell stocks passively on big down days, so the market could face another wave of selling before that pressure is absorbed. Investors focused on long-term holdings appear to still be waiting for market volatility to subside before re-entering.
From a market linkage perspective, the KOSPI has seen three instances this year of a 15% cumulative decline over five trading sessions, and is down about 40% from its record high set in June. It fell 17.11% in the first half of October, the worst among major global stock indices. As one of the bellwethers of the global artificial intelligence trade, whether South Korean stocks can stabilize is a useful reference for the direction of the U.S. chip sector. At present, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has shown early signs of stabilizing, while South Korean stocks are still falling, a divergence in the two markets' trajectories.
For investors, the core contradiction in South Korean stocks right now is the divergence between valuations and liquidity: earnings expectations are being raised and valuations sit at historic lows, but fading buybacks, foreign outflows and potential selling pressure from leveraged funds form a triple drag. Whether the strong rebound in the two memory giants on the 21st can continue depends on whether selling pressure truly fades and when long-term money returns to the market.

SEOUL, - Round-up of South Korean financial markets:
** South Korean shares fell more than 3% on Tuesday to post their lowest close in more than 6 months, as chipmakers dropped on concerns over the global AI investment boom.
** The benchmark KOSPI ended down 215.27 points, or 3.73%, at 5,552.74, after rebounding for two consecutive sessions, and marked its lowest closing level since April 7.
** "The sustainability of the recent rebound was limited as credit and profitability concerns around AI investment remained not fully resolved," said Lee Kyoung-min, an analyst at Daishin Securities.
** The Bank of Korea will keep its key policy rate unchanged on Thursday after two consecutive increases but is expected to raise borrowing costs once more next month, a Reuters poll of economists found, as inflation remains above target and growth remains firm.
** Chipmaker Samsung Electronics fell 2.98%, while peer SK Hynix lost 4.23%.
** Among other index heavyweights, battery maker LG Energy Solution slid 4.17%, while Hyundai Motor and sister automaker Kia Corp were down 4.91% and 3.10%, respectively.
** Steelmaker POSCO Holdings shed 3.97%, while drugmaker Samsung BioLogics fell 2.52%.
** AI infrastructure firm Elice Group plunged more than 30% in its market debut.
** Of the total 915 traded issues, 118 shares advanced, while 773 declined.
** Foreigners were net sellers of shares worth 530.0 billion won ($399.58 million).
** The won was quoted at 1,328.1 per dollar on the onshore settlement platform, 0.38% higher than its previous close at 1,333.1.
** In money and debt markets, December futures on three-year treasury bonds gained 0.09 point to 103.01.
** The most liquid three-year Korean treasury bond yield fell by 2.8 basis points to 3.852%, while the benchmark 10-year yield rose by 3.4 basis points to 4.188%.
($1 = 1,326.4000 won)

high_priority_articles.summary: North Korea-China trade reaches post-Covid high as new border bridge opens  Korea JoongAng Daily
high_priority_articles.full_text:
North Korea and China hold an opening ceremony for the New Yalu River Bridge on Oct. 15 in footage carried by the state-run Korean Central Television on Oct. 16.YONHAP
Trade between North Korea and China reached $2.27 billion in the first nine months of this year, its highest level since the Covid-19 border lockdowns.
The recent opening of the New Yalu River Bridge — connecting the key trading hubs of Sinuiju in North Korea and Dandong in China — has raised expectations of greater cross-border trade and more frequent people-to-people exchanges.
Bilateral trade from January through September rose sharply to $2.27 billion from $1.9 billion during the same period last year, U.S.-based North Korea-focused news site NK News reported Monday, citing data from China's General Administration of Customs.
China's exports to North Korea increased 12.1 percent to $1.79 billion over the same period, while imports from the North surged 50.4 percent to $483.57 million.
Monthly trade also climbed to $299 million in September, up 25.6 percent from $238 million in August. The September figure was the second-highest monthly total this year, behind only April's $326 million.
Experts attribute the rise in bilateral trade to North Korea's increased imports from China and growing exports of light industrial products, including wigs and fake eyelashes, which are not subject to international sanctions.
North Korea imports human hair from China, processes it into wigs and ships the finished products back across the border as part of an active processing trade.
Bilateral trade has risen steadily since Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the North in June. Still, it remains far short of the $4 billion recorded between January and September 2017, when bilateral trade peaked.
Trade plunged after the United Nations Security Council imposed a series of sweeping sanctions on the regime in the second half of 2017 in response to its advancing nuclear and missile programs. It fell further when Pyongyang sealed its borders to prevent the spread of Covid-19.
“Beijing previously took a cautious approach to trade with Pyongyang as it sought to cultivate an image as a responsible major power," Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, said.
"But as its strategic rivalry with the United States has intensified, China has placed greater emphasis on cooperation with North Korea. The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, which connects major overland trade hubs, is likely to further boost trade and people-to-people exchanges between North Korea and China for some time."

South Korea plans $520 billion Samsung and SK hynix chip hub in Gwangju
A public-private push aims to build four AI memory fabs on a former air base, with first mass production targeted for June 2030
South Korea wants its next wave of AI chip wealth to land somewhere other than greater Seoul. The chosen spot is a former military air base in the southwest.
On June 29, 2026, the government unveiled a public-private investment of 800 trillion won, or approximately $520 billion, for a new semiconductor hub in the Gwangju and Jeonnam region. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are set to anchor it.
The plan carries a domestic upside and a diplomatic catch. According to Bloomberg, the hub could help spread AI-driven prosperity into the southwest. It could also become another source of friction between Seoul and Washington.
Four fabs on an old runway
The project centers on the site of the former Gwangju Air Base. That land falls within what is now called the Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City.
Samsung and SK hynix are each expected to build two memory chip fabrication plants there, for four in total.
The schedule runs in stages:
- 2027: site preparation expected to be finished
- 2028: construction could potentially begin
- June 2030: target for first mass production
The initial build-out is planned at about two-thirds the scale of SK hynix’s Yongin complex. Officials have left room for the cluster to grow beyond that first phase.
Why the southwest, and why now
President Lee Jae-myung made the case for the region by pointing to four inputs. He cited water, renewable energy, land and labor as strategic advantages for chip production.

The Seoul metropolitan area has been running short on several of those. Land and resource limits around the capital have become a capacity problem. The Gwangju hub is partly a pressure-release valve.
The project already has visible corporate backing. On October 9, 2026, SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won visited the site and stressed the need to speed up construction.
What this means for chipmakers, the region and Washington
For Samsung and SK hynix, the hub is a bet that AI memory demand stays strong into the next decade. With first production targeted for June 2030, the plants are aimed at demand several years out, not this quarter’s order book.
The scale of the commitment is the headline number to remember. An 800 trillion won public-private package signals that Seoul views AI memory as a national industrial priority, not just a corporate one.
Infrastructure readiness and talent development remain open questions before the cluster can run at full scale.
Watch the 2027 site preparation milestone as the first real test. If that slips, the 2028 construction start and the June 2030 production target come under pressure. The word “potentially” attached to the 2028 date is doing some work.
The Washington dimension is the wild card. Bloomberg flagged the hub as a potential new point of tension in the US-South Korea relationship.
